A1A2: On a wet winter day, Jane hid behind a curtain with a book.
Her aunt kept her away from the other children until she was nicer.
Jane looked at pictures of cold seas, high rocks, and lonely shores.
Her cousin John found her and shouted that she had no money.
John took the heavy book and threw it hard at her head.
Jane's head was bleeding, and she told John he was a cruel boy.
John ran at her, and Jane fought him with all her strength.
Two servants carried Jane upstairs and locked her in the red room.
Nine years before, her uncle had died in that cold, silent room.
Jane screamed to be let out, but her aunt locked her in again.
Jane woke in her own bed, and Bessie sat beside her.
A kind doctor asked her questions, and he said she should go to school.
Bessie brought a sweet cake, but Jane was too sad to eat.
That night, Jane heard the servants say that her parents were poor and dead.
At Christmas, her cousins had gifts and parties, but Jane sat alone.
One day a tall man in black came to the house.
He asked Jane what happens to bad children, and she gave a strange answer.
Her aunt told the man that Jane was a bad, lying child.
When he left, Jane told her aunt that she was the cruel one.
Jane felt proud, then sorry, and Bessie said she was a strange girl.
Before dawn, Jane said goodbye to Bessie and left Gateshead in a coach.
The journey was long, and it was dark and wet when she arrived.
A tall, kind woman called Miss Temple gave her tea and a bed.
In the morning, the water was frozen, and the girls wore brown dresses.
Jane met a thin girl called Helen Burns, who read a book beside her.
A teacher hit Helen with sticks, but Helen did not cry.
Helen told Jane that hate was a waste of a short life.
In winter, the girls were cold and hungry, and they walked far to church.
One day the food was burnt, so Miss Temple gave the girls bread and cheese.
Miss Temple asked Helen and Jane to tea, and Jane saw how clever Helen was.
Jane worked hard, and she hoped that Mr Brocklehurst had forgotten her.
One day he came, and Jane hid, but her slate fell and broke.
He told Miss Temple that bread and cheese was too good for girls.
He said all the girls must have their hair cut short.
He saw Jane and made her stand on a tall stool.
He told the girls that Jane was a liar and must not be spoken to.
Helen walked past and smiled at her, and Jane felt strong again.
At last Jane got down and cried, and Helen held her.
Miss Temple listened to Jane's story and wrote a letter to Mr Lloyd.
His answer said Jane was honest, so Miss Temple told the whole school.
Spring came, but the school was damp, and a fever began.
Jane stayed well and played in the woods, but Helen was sent away.
One night in June, Jane went quietly downstairs to see her friend.
Helen said she was going home to God, and Jane slept beside her.
In the morning, Helen was dead, and Jane cried for many days.
After many deaths, kind men came and built a better, warmer school.
Jane stayed at Lowood for eight years, first as a pupil, then as a teacher.
Miss Temple married and went away, and Jane felt lonely and restless.
Jane wrote to say she wanted work, and a lady named Mrs Fairfax replied.
Bessie came to say goodbye and told her of an uncle far away.
Jane reached the town of Millcote, but no one came for her.
At last a man came with a cart and took her to Thornfield.
In a warm room, a kind old lady in a white cap smiled at her.
The old lady said she was only the housekeeper, and the master was away.
In the morning, Jane saw a big grey house with fields and tall trees.
Jane met her pupil, a little French girl named Adèle, and her nurse.
Adèle told Jane about her mother, who danced, and she sang a song.
Jane began her lessons, and she soon liked the happy little girl.
Mrs Fairfax showed Jane the large, quiet rooms of the house.
On the roof, Jane heard a strange laugh, and Mrs Fairfax said it was Grace Poole.
Winter came, and Jane was happy, but she wanted a bigger life.
On the roof, she wished for adventure, and she heard that strange laugh again.
One cold afternoon, Mrs Fairfax asked Jane to post a letter in Hay.
Jane sat on a gate and remembered old stories about a ghost horse.
Then she heard a horse coming, and a large dog ran past her.
The horse slipped on the ice, and the rider fell down hard.
Jane went to help, and the man put his hand on her shoulder.
He asked where she lived, and Jane told him it was Thornfield.
Jane posted her letter and walked home, feeling that something new had begun.
At home, a doctor was in the hall, and the master had come back.
Jane took Adèle to the dining room, where the master lay on a couch.
Adèle got her gift, and then Mr Rochester looked at Jane.
He asked about her family and her school, and he asked if he was handsome.
Jane said no, and he laughed, because she was so honest.
He asked her to play the piano, but he stopped her after two songs.
He looked at her paintings and asked where she got her strange ideas.
At nine o'clock, he said the paintings were odd and sent her to bed.
Mrs Fairfax said the master was moody, but Jane did not mind his ways.
On other nights, Mr Rochester told Jane about Adèle's mother, a dancer named Céline.
Jane saw that he was kinder than he seemed, and she liked Adèle more.
All winter, Mr Rochester was moody, but he was kind to Jane.
One night, Jane woke and heard a low, wicked laugh at her door.
She opened her door and saw a candle on the floor and smoke.
In his room, the bed was on fire, and Mr Rochester was asleep.
Jane threw water on the bed, and the fire went out.
Mr Rochester told her to wait, and he went upstairs with a candle.
He came back and said that Grace Poole did it, and Jane must tell nobody.
He thanked Jane for saving his life and held her hand for a moment.
In the morning, he was gone, and Grace Poole was calmly sewing a new curtain.
Jane did not understand why Grace was not sent away for the fire.
Mr Rochester went away, and the house felt dull without him.
Mrs Fairfax said he was at a party with the beautiful Miss Ingram.
Jane was angry with herself and drew her own plain face in chalk.
Then she painted a beautiful lady and put the two pictures together.
Soon Mr Rochester came home with many guests, and Jane watched them arrive.
He asked Jane to join the guests, and she sat in a corner.
The ladies said that teachers like Jane were a trouble, and she stayed silent.
Miss Ingram sang beautifully, and Jane left the room alone.
Mr Rochester found her in the hall and asked why she was leaving.
That night Jane knew that she loved her master, and she kept it secret.
While the master was away, an old gypsy woman came to tell fortunes.
The ladies went in one by one, and some came out laughing.
Jane went in last and said she did not believe in fortunes.
The old woman looked at Jane's face and said she was lonely.
Jane knew the voice, and the gypsy was really Mr Rochester.
That night, a pale stranger named Mr Mason came, and Mr Rochester went grey.
At midnight, there was a terrible cry, and the guests woke up afraid.
Mr Rochester took Jane upstairs, where a man lay bleeding in a room.
Jane cared for the man while Mr Rochester went to find a doctor.
At dawn, the doctor came, and the wounded man was sent quietly away.
At sunrise, Mr Rochester walked with Jane and asked a strange question.
Jane said she would feel sorry for a man who made a mistake.
A servant from Gateshead came to the gate with sad news.
John Reed was dead, and his mother was ill and called for Jane.
Jane asked the master to let her visit her sick aunt.
Jane packed her bag, and Mr Rochester said that she must come back.
Jane rode all day in a coach and reached Gateshead in the evening.
Bessie met her at the gate, and they walked up to the house together.
Her cousins wore black and spoke to her coldly.
Her aunt lay in bed, thin and hard, and she looked at Jane.
Jane stayed at Gateshead while Georgiana complained and Eliza kept to her rules.
At last her aunt said she had done Jane a wrong.
Three years before, Jane's uncle wrote to ask for her, and her aunt lied.
Her aunt said she hated Jane, and she gave Jane the letter.
Jane said she was sorry, but her aunt turned her face away.
That night Mrs Reed died, and Jane sat beside her, feeling sad.
After the funeral, Eliza said that she would go into a convent.
Georgiana went to London, and the two sisters said goodbye without a kiss.
Jane took the coach to Thornfield and wondered if Mr Rochester was married.
On a summer evening, she saw Mr Rochester sitting on a gate.
Mr Rochester held out his hands and said that he was glad she was home.
Thornfield felt like home, and Mrs Fairfax and Adèle were very happy.
One evening, Mr Rochester said he was going to marry soon.
He said that Jane must go to Ireland, far across the sea.
Jane stood under a big tree and cried at the thought.
She told him that she was not a machine, and she was his equal.
Mr Rochester took her hands and said that he loved her.
Jane thought he was joking, but he said Miss Ingram meant nothing to him.
Jane saw that he was serious, and she said yes.
A storm came, and lightning broke the great tree in two.
Mr Rochester bought Jane silks and jewels, but she did not like them.
Jane wrote to her uncle in Madeira, hoping to have some money of her own.
Mrs Fairfax told Jane to be careful, because masters and servants are not equal.
Jane teased him gently and said that she would not become a fine lady.
The night before the wedding, a storm shook the house, and he was away.
At midnight, a tall, strange woman came into Jane's room and held up the veil.
The woman tore the veil in two, and Jane fainted.
In the morning, Mr Rochester said that it was partly a dream.
On the wedding day, Jane wore a plain white dress, and they hurried to church.
The priest asked if anyone knew a reason not to marry, and a stranger spoke.
The lawyer said that Mr Rochester already had a wife.
Mr Rochester said the wedding must stop, and he led them all home.
A man from Jamaica said that his sister lived at Thornfield.
Mr Rochester led them up to a secret door at the top of the house.
In the dark room, a strange figure was moving on the floor.
The figure jumped on Mr Rochester, and he held her tightly.
Mr Rochester said, “This is my wife,” and Jane went to her room alone.
Mr Rochester told her the story of his marriage in Jamaica.
He asked her to live with him in France, but it was wrong.
Jane said no, and she decided to leave Thornfield in the night.
Before dawn, Jane packed a small bundle and kissed Adèle goodbye.
She passed Mr Rochester's door in silence and left by a side door.
She took the first coach and paid all her money for the fare.
Two days later, she got down at Whitcross and had left her bundle behind.
She walked onto the moor and slept in the heather.
In the village, nobody would give her food for her gloves.
At a farm, a kind woman gave her a slice of bread.
She slept in a wet wood that night and was too weak to go on.
On the third night, she saw a far light and walked toward it.
At the house, an old servant sent her away, and Jane fell down.
Jane cried at the door, and a man named St John carried her in.
The man's sisters gave her bread and milk, and she used a false name.
Jane stayed in bed for three days, and the old servant said she was sorry.
As she got better, she learned that the family was poor but clever.
The sisters taught her German, and she loved them dearly.
St John asked what she could do, and he offered her a teacher's job.
She took the job and got a small cottage with two rooms.
Thirty poor village girls came to her school, and they were rough and slow.
A rich, kind girl named Rosamond Oliver visited the school.
Jane saw that St John loved Rosamond, but he would not marry her.
Jane drew Rosamond's face, and St John tore a piece of the paper.
On a snowy night, St John came and said he knew her true name.
He said that her uncle John Eyre had died and left her much money.
St John said that John Eyre was his uncle too, so they were cousins.
Jane was so happy to have a family, and she shared her money equally.
At Christmas, Jane made Moor House a happy home for them all.
Jane closed her school, and St John taught her a language of India.
St John asked her to marry him and go to India.
Jane said she would go as his sister, and he prayed over her.
That night, Jane heard Mr Rochester's voice call her name from far away.
In the morning, Jane left St John to find out about Mr Rochester.
She came to Thornfield and found only black, burned walls.
At the inn, a man said that Bertha set the fire and died in it.
Mr Rochester lost his sight and a hand, and he lived far away.
Jane took a carriage through dark woods to his old house, Ferndean.
Jane brought a tray into the room and saw him sitting by the fire.
He heard her voice and thought it was a dream, so he touched her face.
He feared that she only felt sorry for him, but she said she would stay.
Jane and Mr Rochester were married quietly in a small church.
Jane was happy for ten years, and St John went on working in India.
B1B2: It was a wet November afternoon, too cold for a walk, so Jane hid in a window seat. She pulled the red curtain across and opened a book of bird pictures.
On the other side of the curtain, her cousins Eliza, John and Georgiana sat by the fire with their mother. Mrs Reed said that Jane must keep apart until she learned to be more cheerful and childlike.
Jane turned the pages slowly, looking at pictures of icy seas, lonely rocks and far northern shores. She liked to imagine those wild places because they were so far away from Gateshead Hall.

Suddenly the curtain was pulled back, and her fourteen-year-old cousin John stood there, large and red-faced. He laughed at her and said that she was a poor orphan with no money and no right to the books in that house.
John snatched the book from her hands and threw it with all his strength. It struck Jane on the head, and she fell against the door and cut herself.
Jane's temper flared, and she told John that he was a cruel, wicked boy, as bad as a murderer. He rushed at her, and she fought back as hard as she could.
Mrs Reed called for the servants, Bessie and Miss Abbot, who took hold of Jane. Although she struggled, they carried her upstairs, and her aunt ordered them to lock her in the red-room.
The red-room was a large, cold bedroom with a great bed hung with deep red curtains. Nobody slept there any more, because Mr Reed, Jane's uncle, had died in it nine years before.
Jane saw her own pale face in the tall mirror, and it looked like a small, strange ghost. She wondered whether her uncle's spirit might return to punish those who had been unkind to his niece.
A pale light moved across the wall, and Jane, wild with fear, screamed and begged to be let out. Mrs Reed only pushed her back and locked the door, and Jane fainted.
Jane woke in her own bed, with a warm fire glowing and Bessie sitting beside her. Her head ached, her whole body was weak, and she began to cry without knowing why.

A kind gentleman, Mr Lloyd the apothecary, sat by the bed and asked what had made her so ill. When Jane told him about the red-room, he said that she might be happier at school, and Jane agreed with all her heart.
Bessie brought a tart on a pretty plate, which once would have made Jane very happy. Now she could not eat it, so Bessie sang her a sad old song about a poor orphan child.
That night, as the servants talked quietly beside the candle, Jane heard something she had never known. Her poor parents, a clergyman and his wife, had both died of fever when Jane was a baby.

Christmas came, and Mrs Reed's children enjoyed presents, parties and good food in the warm drawing-room. Jane was not invited to join them, so she sat alone in the nursery with her old doll and her books.

One morning, a tall man in black stood on the carpet in the breakfast-room, as stiff and cold as a pillar. This was Mr Brocklehurst, who owned Lowood School, and Mrs Reed had asked him to take Jane as a pupil.
He asked Jane whether she knew where bad children go after they die, and she said they go to hell. When he asked how she could avoid it, she answered that she must keep in good health and not die.

Mrs Reed told him that Jane had a deceitful nature, which he must warn her teachers about. Mr Brocklehurst agreed gravely, saying that liars would be punished and that Jane would be watched closely at Lowood.

When he had gone, Jane felt something burst inside her, and she faced her aunt with shaking hands. She said that she was not deceitful, that Mrs Reed was the cruel one, and that she would never call her aunt again.
At first Jane felt like a winner, but soon the feeling turned sour, and she was sorry she had spoken. Bessie sat beside her in the dusk and said that she was a strange, solitary little thing.

Jane woke before dawn, dressed by candlelight and said goodbye to Bessie, who kissed her at the gate. The house was still asleep, and she left Gateshead by coach without seeing her aunt or her cousins.
The journey seemed endless, and the day grew darker as the coach passed through towns and over hills. It was night, and rain was falling hard, when at last Jane was set down at the gates of Lowood.

A servant led her through the dark corridors to a room with a bright fire, where two ladies were sitting. One of them, Miss Temple, was tall, fair and gentle, and she gave Jane tea and bread before putting her to bed.

A bell woke the school in the dark, and Jane found that the water in the jugs had frozen overnight. Eighty girls in brown dresses stood in cold rows to pray, and then they were given porridge so burnt that few could eat it.

That afternoon Jane noticed a thin girl with a book, sitting alone beside the window, and she asked what it was. The girl, Helen Burns, explained that Lowood was a charity school, which was paid for by kind people and run by Mr Brocklehurst.

Their teacher, Miss Scatcherd, found fault with Helen's dirty nails and hit her neck with a bundle of twigs. Jane waited for the tears, but Helen only stood calmly, and Jane burned with anger on her behalf.
Later Jane asked Helen how she could bear such cruelty without a word. Helen replied that life is too short for hatred, and that the Bible tells us to forgive our enemies, even when it is hard.

The winter at Lowood was bitter, with thin meals, chilblains and rooms that never grew warm. On Sundays the girls walked two miles to church in the snow, and they ate a cold lunch there before walking back.

On one terrible morning the porridge was so badly burnt that no one could swallow it, and the girls stayed hungry until noon. Miss Temple saw their misery and ordered bread and cheese for everyone, paying for it herself without asking permission.

Miss Temple invited Helen and Jane into her own room, where she served tea and seed-cake as if they were grown women. Jane listened with wonder as Helen spoke of history and poetry, for she had never imagined that anyone so untidy could be so brilliant.
The weeks passed, and Jane worked so hard that she rose steadily in her class. She began to hope that Mr Brocklehurst had forgotten about her, because nothing had been said since she arrived.
One afternoon the tall man in black walked into the schoolroom, and Jane tried to hide her face behind her slate. In her fright she let it slip, and it fell to the floor and broke with a loud crack.

Mr Brocklehurst spoke severely to Miss Temple about the bread and cheese she had served, saying that the girls must learn to bear hunger. Miss Temple answered with calm dignity, although her face grew as pale and hard as marble.

Then he spotted a girl with curly hair, and he ordered that every girl's hair be cut off at once. At that moment his wife and daughters swept into the room in fine silk and velvet, which seemed a strange thing for such preachers.
His sharp eyes found Jane, and he said that this was the girl with the broken slate. He ordered her to be brought forward, and two teachers placed her on a tall stool in front of the whole school.

Mr Brocklehurst told the girls that Jane looked like an ordinary child, but that the devil had already entered her. He said that she was a liar, and that no one was to speak to her for the rest of the day.
Jane thought that she would sink into the floor, but Helen passed by and gave her a warm, bright smile. That look was like a ray of light, and it gave Jane the strength to keep standing.

When half an hour had passed, the girls were let go, and Jane crept into the dim corridor and began to cry. Helen came to find her, and she held her tight and told her that the right people would not believe it.

That evening Miss Temple called Jane to her room and asked to hear her side of the story. Jane told her everything calmly, and Miss Temple promised to write to Mr Lloyd, the apothecary, to learn whether it was true.
Mr Lloyd's reply came within a few days, and it said that Jane had spoken the truth. Miss Temple then told the whole school that Jane had never been a liar, and Jane felt lighter.
In spring the hills around Lowood turned green, and flowers opened in the woods. But the school stood in a damp hollow, and before long a fever began to spread among the girls.

Jane stayed well and was free to wander through the sunny woods, because the classes had nearly stopped. Helen, who had a long illness in her lungs, was moved into a separate room, and Jane was not allowed to see her.

One warm evening in June, Jane learned that Helen was very ill, and she could not sleep. She waited until the house was quiet, then crept downstairs in her nightdress to find her friend in Miss Temple's room.
Helen was thin and weak, but she smiled and said that she was glad to see her. She said she was going home to God without fear, and Jane fell asleep in her arms.

In the morning Jane woke and found that Helen had died peacefully during the night. She was buried in a small churchyard, and many years later Jane placed a stone there that bore her name and the word Resurgam.

So many girls had died that some important men began to ask how Lowood was being run. They found that the food was bad, the building was damp and the school had been badly managed, so a new, kinder committee took over.
Lowood now became a good and useful school, with warm rooms and decent meals. Jane worked hard and spent six years as a pupil and then two as a teacher, always supported by Miss Temple.
When Miss Temple married a clergyman and moved far away, Jane felt that all her calm had gone with her. For the first time in years she looked beyond the green hills and longed for the real world.

Jane prayed for a new life, and one night an idea came to her: she could advertise for a post as a governess. She wrote the notice, and after a few days, a lady named Mrs Fairfax replied from a house called Thornfield.

Just before she left, Bessie came to visit, now married and a mother, and she was proud to see how Jane had grown. She told her that Jane's cousins were well, and that years ago an uncle called John Eyre had come asking for her from Madeira.
After a long day on the coach, Jane arrived at an inn in Millcote, but nobody had come from Thornfield to meet her. She sat alone with her trunk and wondered whether she had made a terrible mistake.
After an hour a man called John arrived with a cart and loaded her trunk without a word. They drove for ten miles through dark lanes, and Jane could see nothing but the swinging light of the lantern.
At last the cart stopped at a large door, and Jane was led into a bright, warm parlour. A small, neat old lady in a white cap sat knitting by the fire, and Jane took her for the mistress.

Mrs Fairfax gave Jane tea and cake, and she explained that she was only the housekeeper and a distant relation of the family. The master, Mr Rochester, was often away for months, and he had left his young ward in her care.

When Jane woke the next morning, the sun was shining, and she looked out at the house for the first time. It was old and grey, with battlements along the roof, and beyond it lay green fields, tall trees and a noisy colony of rooks.

After breakfast Jane met her pupil, a pretty little girl of about eight called Adèle Varens. She spoke mostly French, and she had a French nurse named Sophie, but Jane had learned the language well at Lowood.

Adèle chattered about her mother, who was an opera dancer in Paris, and she sang a song from the theatre in a high, sweet voice. Jane listened and thought that it was a strange thing for a child to know so well.

Jane began the lessons the same morning, and she found that Adèle was lively and affectionate but not especially clever. However, the child tried hard, and within a week Jane had grown quite fond of her.

Mrs Fairfax took Jane through the house, showing her the library, the dining room and the splendid bedrooms. Everything was spotless and ready for visitors, yet the master hardly ever came, and the rooms were mostly silent.

At the end of the tour they climbed to the roof, where Jane gazed out at the hills and the village in the distance. On the way down, she heard a low laugh, and Mrs Fairfax said it was only Grace Poole, who sewed there.

The months passed quietly at Thornfield, and Jane was comfortable, although the days were all alike. In the evenings she walked the long corridor on the third floor and felt that something in her was waiting.

She stood on the roof one afternoon, looking at the far blue hills, and wished that she could see more of the world. As she went down, the same slow, strange laugh came again from behind a low black door.

On a cold January afternoon, Mrs Fairfax asked Jane to post a letter in the village of Hay, about two miles away. Jane put on her cloak and bonnet and set off down the frosty lane with the sun sinking behind the hills.

The lane was silent, and Jane sat down on a stile to rest while the light faded. She remembered a story from Bessie about the Gytrash, a spirit that haunted lonely roads in the shape of a horse or a large dog.
As she was thinking of it, she heard the slow thud of hooves on the hard ground. First a great dog with a black and white coat trotted past her, and then a horse and rider came round the bend.
The horse stepped on a patch of ice and slipped, and the rider was thrown down with a heavy crash. The dog barked loudly, and the sound echoed across the empty fields.

Jane ran to him and asked whether he was hurt, and he muttered something that sounded like a curse. He had sprained his ankle, and he leaned on her shoulder, which was rather rough, while he limped to his horse.
The man was dark and broad, with a stern face and heavy brows, and he was not young. He asked where she lived, and when she said she was the governess at Thornfield, he only looked at her.

He mounted his horse in spite of the pain, thanked her shortly and rode away with the dog at his side. Jane posted her letter, and as she walked home under the rising moon, she felt her quiet life had been shaken.

When she reached Thornfield, there was a strange gig outside, and a man was talking in the hall with a surgeon named Mr Carter. Mrs Fairfax told her that the master had just arrived, that his horse had fallen on the ice, and that he had hurt his ankle.

After tea, Jane took Adèle down to the dining room, where the master of Thornfield lay on a couch with his foot on a cushion. His large dog, Pilot, lay beside him, and Mr Rochester did not look up when they came in.

Adèle had been asking all day about her present, and when it was brought to her, she hugged the box with delight. Only then did Mr Rochester turn his dark face to Jane and tell her to draw her chair nearer to the fire.
He asked her where her parents had lived, how long she had been at Lowood and what she had learned there. Then, without a smile, he asked whether she thought him handsome.

Jane replied calmly that she did not, and the answer was out before she could stop it. To her surprise Mr Rochester burst out laughing, and said that she was as direct as a child but not at all childish.

He told her to sit at the piano and play something, and she played two short pieces as well as she could. He listened with his head to one side, and then he said that it was enough and that she was clearly no genius.

Mr Rochester asked to see the paintings that Jane had brought with her, and she fetched three watercolours from her portfolio. He looked at them for a long time, holding each one to the lamp, and he asked who had given her these strange visions.

Jane said that the ideas had come out of her own head, and he answered that this was what he feared. Then he looked at the clock, said that she was tired and that the child should be in bed, and dismissed them both.

Mrs Fairfax told Jane that the master was moody and had suffered much from his family. Jane thought about it for some time, but she decided that she did not mind his temper, because she preferred honest roughness to false kindness.

On the next few evenings, the master sent for her and talked with her by the fire while his dog slept on the rug. He told her about Céline Varens, the French dancer he had loved, who had deceived him and then left Adèle behind.

He did not believe that Adèle was his daughter, but he had taken her in and given her a home in England. Jane saw that the stern man had a kinder heart than he showed, and she felt tender toward the little girl.

As the winter went on, Mr Rochester remained moody, sometimes passing Jane without a word and sometimes talking with her for hours. She found that with her he was more open than with anyone else, and she began to look forward to the evenings.
One night Jane woke in the dark, sure that she had heard something close to her door. There was a murmur, then a low, wicked laugh that made her blood run cold, and footsteps that slowly went away.
She put on her dressing gown and opened the door, and at her feet she found a candle burning on the floor. The passage was full of smoke, and the smoke was drifting out of Mr Rochester's room.
She ran inside and found the bed curtains in flames, with the fire already climbing over the bed. Mr Rochester lay in the middle of it, fast asleep in a heavy, unnatural slumber.

Jane called his name and shook him, but he did not wake, so she seized the basin and the jug from the washstand. She poured every drop over the bed and over him, and the water put out the flames with a great hiss.
Mr Rochester woke, spluttering and furious, and asked what was happening. When Jane had told him, he put on a coat, asked her to wait and went upstairs with a candle.

Jane stood shivering in the dark for what felt like hours before the light came back down. He said that it was just as he feared, that it was Grace Poole, and that Jane must say nothing about it to anyone.
Then he looked at her seriously and said that she had saved his life and that he owed her a great debt. He held her hand for a moment, longer than was necessary, and told her to go to bed.

Jane hardly slept, and when she came down in the morning, she learned that Mr Rochester had left the house at dawn. In his bedroom she found Grace Poole sitting by the window, sewing a new curtain as if nothing had happened.

Jane watched the woman's plain, blank face and waited for her to say something about the fire. But Grace only said that her master should not sleep with a candle, and Jane wondered why she was not sent away.

Mr Rochester had been away for more than two weeks, and Thornfield seemed to Jane duller than it had ever been. She had not expected to miss him so much, and she was a little frightened by the feeling.

Mrs Fairfax said that he was at a large house party, where a young lady named Blanche Ingram was also staying. She was tall, rich and beautiful, the housekeeper said, and she might well become the next mistress of Thornfield.

Jane was angry with herself for thinking of him, and she decided to give herself a lesson. She took a piece of chalk and drew her own face, plain and thin and pale, and wrote beneath it Governess, Poor and Plain.

Then she took an ivory panel and her best paints and painted Blanche as she imagined her, with dark curls. She set it beside the chalk drawing and told herself that this was how she should always think of the two women.

A few days later Mrs Fairfax announced that Mr Rochester was coming home, and that he was bringing a large party with him. Jane watched from the gallery as the carriages arrived, and she saw fine ladies in riding habits step down and sweep into the house.

In the evening Mr Rochester sent word that Jane and Adèle were to join the guests in the drawing room, and she obeyed unwillingly. She slipped into a seat in a window recess and kept a book in front of her, so that she could watch without being noticed.

The ladies were beautiful and richly dressed, and they spoke freely about anything that came into their heads. Lady Ingram said that governesses were a horrid nuisance, and the others laughed and agreed, but Jane said nothing and went on reading.

Blanche Ingram sat at the grand piano and sang in a rich, strong voice, with Mr Rochester standing beside her. As the guests applauded, Jane felt a heaviness she could not explain, and she rose and slipped quietly out of the room.

She had almost reached the stairs when Mr Rochester came out into the hall and caught up with her. He asked why she had not wished him good evening, and she answered, with a polite smile, that she had not wanted to disturb him.

He said she looked pale and low, and that she should take care of herself, and then he let her go. On the stairs Jane understood that she loved him, and that it was the best and worst thing to happen to her.

Mr Rochester had gone to Millcote on business, and the guests were bored without him. Then a servant announced that an old gypsy woman had come to the door and wanted to tell the ladies their fortunes.
She was shown into the library, and the young ladies went in to see her, one at a time. Some came out laughing, and others looked quiet and thoughtful, and nobody would say what she had told them.

At last a message came for Jane, and she went in and sat on the other side of the fire. The old woman wore a red cloak and a broad hat, and Jane told her calmly that she did not believe in fortune-telling.

The gypsy looked at her face and said that she was cold, sick and silly, but that she hid a secret hope in her heart. Jane smiled, said that she knew no such thing, and answered each question with care.

Jane began to notice the shape of the hands and the sound of the voice, and she thought that she knew them well. Then the old woman threw off her hat and cloak, and there was Mr Rochester, laughing at his own joke.

That same evening a stranger arrived at the house, a pale, tired gentleman named Mr Mason who had just come from Jamaica. Mr Rochester went grey when he heard the name, but he forced himself to give a warm welcome.

At midnight the whole house was woken by a terrible cry from the third floor, and the guests ran out in their nightclothes. Mr Rochester came among them calmly and said that a servant had had a bad dream, and he persuaded them to go back to bed.

Soon afterwards he found Jane in the passage, and he asked her to bring a sponge and some water quietly. He led her up to the third floor, where he opened a secret room, and there lay Mr Mason, bleeding from the arm.

Mr Rochester told her to guard the man while he fetched the surgeon, and to let him say nothing. From the next room Jane heard a low snarl and the sound of something moving, and she did not dare to turn her head.

Mr Carter, the surgeon, arrived at dawn and dressed the wound, and he said that it looked as if the man had been bitten. Before any of the guests woke, Mr Rochester helped Mr Mason into a carriage and sent him quietly away.
At sunrise Mr Rochester walked with Jane in the garden, among the roses and the wet green grass. He asked her a strange question about a man who had made a terrible mistake when he was young.
Jane answered that she would pity such a man, and she believed that he might still find a way to be good. Mr Rochester said that her words gave him comfort, but he did not tell her what he meant.
A few days later a servant in black came to the gate, asking for Miss Eyre, and he turned out to be Robert Leaven. He was the coachman at Gateshead, and he had ridden a long way to bring bad news.
He told Jane that her cousin John had led a wild life and was now dead. His mother had been so shocked that she had had a stroke, and she kept asking for Jane.
Jane went to Mr Rochester in the library and asked him for leave to visit her sick aunt. He joked that she might run away, but in the end he agreed, and he told her how long she could stay.
She packed a small trunk that evening, while Adèle watched and asked a hundred questions. Mr Rochester told her gravely that she was to come back, and she promised him that she would.
Early the next morning she took the coach, and it rolled all day along wide roads through green fields. Jane felt strange, because she was going back to the house that she had left as a lonely child.

At the lodge gate she saw a woman in a bonnet waiting for her, and it was Bessie, now stouter and kinder than ever. They hugged and talked all the way up the drive, and Jane felt that one person truly welcomed her.
In the drawing room, Jane's two cousins sat sewing in black dresses. Eliza was pale and stern and Georgiana was pretty and bored, and they greeted her with a few cold words.
Mrs Reed lay propped on the pillows in the same large bedroom. She was thin and hard-faced, but her eyes were sharp, and she asked whether this tall young woman was really her niece.
Jane stayed on at Gateshead for a month, as Mrs Reed grew weaker. Georgiana complained all day, while Eliza kept strictly to her own routine, and neither of them paid any attention to their mother.
One night Mrs Reed asked Jane to come close to the bed, and she said that she had done her a wrong. She wanted to speak about it before she died.
Three years before, she said, a letter had come from Jane's uncle, John Eyre, in Madeira. He had wished to adopt Jane and leave her all his fortune, but Mrs Reed had written back that Jane was dead.
She confessed that she had never been able to forgive Jane, because her husband had loved the child so much. Then she took the letter from a drawer and gave it to Jane with a shaking hand.
Jane forgave her, from her heart, and asked her aunt to forgive her too. But Mrs Reed only turned her face away and said that Jane had a bad disposition, and that she had always disliked her.
That night Mrs Reed died, and Jane sat by her bed with a candle until morning. She felt no anger, only a deep sadness that her aunt could not have been kinder.

After the funeral Eliza told Jane that she planned to enter a convent in France, and she spoke with great calm. She had put her desk in order, locked up the house and arranged everything for her new life.

Georgiana wanted to go to London and marry a rich man, and she thought of nothing else. The two sisters said goodbye with hardly a kiss, and Jane saw that they had never been truly fond of each other.
Jane took the coach to Thornfield after a month away, with her heart beating quickly. She wondered whether Mr Rochester had already married Miss Ingram, and how she would bear to see it.
On a warm summer evening Jane left the coach at Millcote and walked home across the fields. The air smelled of fresh hay, and by a gate she saw a man in a dark cloak sitting with a book.

Mr Rochester jumped up from the stile, took both of her hands and said that he had known she would come back. He told her that he had missed her badly, and that Thornfield had seemed empty without her.

At the house, Mrs Fairfax and Adèle ran to meet her, and Jane felt that she had come home at last. For several days she was happy, and she tried not to think about the wedding that must surely be coming.

One warm evening, Jane was walking in the orchard when Mr Rochester came to join her, and he spoke quietly. He told her that he was going to be married soon, and that she would have to leave Thornfield.

He said that he had heard of a post for her in Ireland, with a lady named Mrs O'Gall and her five daughters. It was a long way off, he said, with a great sea between them, and perhaps they would never meet again.
Jane stopped under a great chestnut tree, and the tears ran down her face. She tried to speak calmly, but she could not hide how much it hurt her to leave the house and the man she loved.
At last she spoke, and the words came out of her like a flood. She said that she was not a machine without feelings, and that in spirit she was as good as he was.

Rochester took her hands in the twilight and said that his bride was beside him, and that he meant to marry Jane herself. Jane thought that he was mocking her, and she turned away, but he swore that he loved her.
She told him that it was cruel to joke, and that Miss Ingram would never allow it. He answered that he had only pretended to love Blanche, who cared for nothing but his money.

Jane looked into his face and saw that it was full of honest feeling, and she felt joy spread through her like light. She said yes, and he held her close, and for a few minutes the whole garden seemed to be singing.

While they stood under the tree, the wind rose, thunder rolled in the sky and the rain began to pour. They ran for the house, and behind them a flash of lightning struck the great chestnut tree and split it in two.
Mr Rochester took Jane to Millcote and bought her silks, jewels and a beautiful veil. Jane did not enjoy it, because she felt like a doll, and she begged him to stop.

She wrote to her uncle, John Eyre, in Madeira, telling him that she was alive and that she was going to be married. She hoped that he might leave her a little money, so that she would not come to her husband quite empty-handed.
Mrs Fairfax spoke to her gently one afternoon and said that she must be careful. A master and a governess were not equals, she said, and men often forgot their promises.
Jane smiled and told her that she would stay herself, and that she would not become a fine lady for anyone. Mr Rochester only laughed when she told him, and said that he loved her just as she was.

The wedding was to take place in four weeks, and the night before it, Mr Rochester was called away on business. A wind began to blow around Thornfield, and Jane could not sleep, though everything was ready for the morning.
At midnight the door opened, and a tall, dark woman came in with a candle in her hand. She took the wedding veil from the wardrobe, put it on her own head and looked at herself in the mirror.
Her face was wild and red, her eyes were dark, and her long hair hung down her back. Then she tore the veil in two, threw it on the floor and bent over Jane's bed, and Jane fainted.
When Jane woke it was morning, and Mr Rochester was sitting beside her, holding her hand. He said it was partly a dream, but the veil was real, and he would explain in a year and a day.
On the wedding morning Jane put on a plain white dress, and she and Mr Rochester walked quickly to the little church. Mrs Fairfax and Adèle watched them go, and nobody else was invited.

The vicar read the service, and then he asked whether anyone present knew any reason why the two should not be married. A voice from the back of the church answered, and a man in a dark coat stood up.
The man in the dark coat was Mr Briggs, a lawyer, and he said that the wedding could not go on. Mr Rochester was already married, he said, to Bertha Mason, who was still alive at Thornfield Hall.
Mr Rochester did not deny it, and his face turned hard and dark. He told the vicar to close the book, and he asked everyone to follow him to the house.

A pale man stepped up beside the lawyer, and Jane saw that it was Mr Mason, who had been hurt at Thornfield. He said that Bertha was his sister, that she was living in the house and that he had seen her there himself.
Mr Rochester led the whole party up to the third floor, past Jane's bedroom and past the rooms of the house. At the end of a passage he lifted a tapestry and unlocked a small black door.
Inside was a room with no daylight, lit only by a fire, and Grace Poole sat by it. In the dark corner something moved on all fours, like a wild animal, with a long mane of grey hair.
The figure sprang up and rushed at Mr Rochester, who was a strong man, and he fought to hold her. At last he tied her to a chair, while she snarled and struggled against the ropes.
He turned to the shocked guests and said in a low, bitter voice, “This is my wife.” Jane went back to her room in a daze, shut the door and sat down.

Later that day Mr Rochester came and knocked at her door, and she let him in. He told her that his father had arranged his marriage to Bertha for her money, and that she had gone mad within a few years.

He had kept her in Thornfield, in the care of Grace Poole, because he could not bear to send her to an asylum. Now he begged Jane to leave England with him and live as his wife, although the law would never call her so.

Jane wept, but she knew that she could not say yes, and she told him so plainly. She cared about herself and her own self-respect, and she knew that she must go away from Thornfield before the morning.
Before dawn Jane packed a small bundle and took twenty shillings from her purse. She kissed Adèle gently as she slept, and she looked at her own plain face in the mirror for the last time.

She crept past Mr Rochester's door, where she thought she could hear him breathing, and went down to the kitchen. A moment later she was outside, and she walked across the cold grass without looking back.
She hurried two miles to a crossroads, where she took the first coach that came by. She gave the driver every shilling she had, and she did not even ask where he was going.
Two days later the coach set her down at a place called Whitcross, which was nothing but a signpost on a lonely moor. Only then did she find that she had left her little bundle behind in the coach.
She had no money and no food, so she walked out onto the moor, which was purple with heather. When night came she found a hollow among the stones and lay down, and she cried herself to sleep.

In the morning she walked to a village, and she tried to sell her handkerchief for something to eat. Nobody wanted it, and the baker, who looked at her with suspicion, said that he had nothing for beggars.
At a farm she asked a woman for a little work, and the woman, who was kind, gave her a slice of bread. Jane ate it by the roadside, and it was the first thing she had eaten in two days.
That night it rained, and she crept into a wet wood and lay down under a tree. She was so cold and weak that she thought she might not wake again.
On the third night she saw a light shining far across the moor, and she got up and walked toward it, falling many times. It took her hours to cross the marsh, but she did not stop.
At last she came to a house called Marsh End, and she knocked at the door in the storm. An old servant opened it, but she said that she could not take in beggars, and she shut the door in her face.
A voice behind her said that she must not die at the door, and a tall young man lifted her in his arms. His name was St John Rivers, and he carried her into the warm kitchen.
His sisters, Diana and Mary, gave her bread and milk and looked after her kindly. When they asked her name, she said that it was Jane Elliott, because she was afraid that Mr Rochester might find her.
Jane lay in bed for three days, too weak to speak. When Hannah, the old servant, came to see her, she said that she was sorry for sending her away.

As she grew stronger, Jane learned that the two sisters were poor but very clever, and that they had read many books. Their father had just died, and they were working as governesses in the south, with only a few weeks at home.
In the evenings Diana and Mary taught Jane German, and she soon loved them as sisters. Their brother, the clergyman, was cold and silent, and he spent his time reading in the study.

One day St John asked Jane what work she could do, and she said that she would do anything honest. He told her that a new school for girls was about to open in Morton, and he offered her the post of teacher.
Jane accepted gratefully, and he found her a little cottage near the school. It had two small rooms, with a bed, a table and two chairs, and Jane thought it was a good beginning.

On the first morning thirty poor village girls came to the schoolroom, and they were rough and slow and could hardly read. Jane worked hard, but she felt that she had come down far from the fine rooms of Thornfield.

One afternoon a lovely young woman in a bright bonnet walked into the schoolroom, and Jane learned that she was Rosamond Oliver. She was the daughter of the richest man in Morton, and she was as kind as she was beautiful.

Jane soon noticed that St John could not take his eyes off Rosamond, and that he loved her very much. But he said that he would never marry her, because he meant to be a missionary, and Rosamond was not strong enough for that.
One afternoon Jane painted a portrait of Rosamond Oliver, and St John looked at it for a long time. Then he tore a narrow strip from the paper that lay beside it and put it in his pocket.
A few days later, on a snowy evening, he came to Jane's cottage and asked her to say who she truly was. He held up the strip of paper, and on it was written the name Jane Eyre.

Jane admitted that it was her name, and he told her that a lawyer named Mr Briggs had been searching for her. Her uncle, John Eyre, had died in Madeira, and he had left her everything, which was twenty thousand pounds.
She asked how he knew so much about it, and he smiled for the first time. John Eyre was the brother of his own mother, he said, and that made Jane his cousin.
Jane laughed and cried at once, because she had never in her life had a family. She said that the fortune must be shared in four equal parts, and in the end Diana, Mary and St John agreed.
At Christmas the cousins gathered at Moor House, and Jane cleaned and baked and made the old rooms bright and warm. She had never been so happy, and she felt that she had found her real home.

In the spring Jane closed her school, and the village girls came to say goodbye, with Rosamond in tears. St John began teaching Jane a language of India called Hindustani, because he meant to leave for the East.
After some weeks he asked Jane to marry him and come with him to India as a missionary's wife. He said that she was made for work, not for love, and that God had chosen her for the task.

Jane replied that she would go as his sister, but she would not marry a man who did not love her. He grew cold and angry, but he knelt to pray with his hand on her head, and she felt her will begin to waver.
She whispered to heaven for a sign, and in that instant the whole room seemed to shake. A voice that she knew called her name three times, and it was Mr Rochester's, and it came from far away.
The next morning Jane told St John that she had heard a voice, and that she must find out what had happened to Mr Rochester. He said nothing, and she left at once by the coach.
After a long journey she reached Thornfield, and she ran across the fields to see the house. But where it had stood there was only a black ruin, with empty windows and no roof.
She went to the inn nearby and asked the landlord what had happened. He told her that a madwoman named Bertha had set fire to the house one night, and that she had died in the flames.
Mr Rochester had helped everyone out, the landlord said, and had gone back for his wife. A falling beam had blinded him and crushed his hand, and now he lived alone at Ferndean, thirty miles away.
Jane hired a carriage that very evening and travelled to Ferndean. The house was old and damp, hidden in a wood, and an old servant named Mary opened the door and stared at her.
Mary was just carrying a tray into the parlour, so Jane took it from her and went in. Mr Rochester was sitting beside a low fire, blind and silent, with his head bowed.
She spoke to him, and he jumped up and asked whether he was dreaming. He touched her hands and face to be sure, and then he took her in his arms.
He said that he feared she pitied him, because he was blind and broken, and he told her to go. But Jane said that she was free, that she was rich, and that she wanted to stay and care for him.
He asked her to marry him, and this time she said yes with all her heart. They were married quietly in the old church, and Jane tells her readers simply that she married him.
Jane writes that they have been very happy for ten years, and that Adèle has grown up kind and good. Rochester saw his first son, and St John's letters from India say that his work is nearly done.
