This was Mr Brocklehurst, the master of a charity school called Lowood, and his long, severe face and large teeth gave her no comfort whatever. Mrs Reed, who had arranged the visit, sat by the fire with her hands folded and looked at Jane as though she were a stain on the carpet.

He began by asking her if she knew what became of the wicked after death, and she told him, in a small steady voice, that they went to hell. When he asked what she would do to escape such a fate, she answered with perfect honesty that she must keep in good health and not die. The visitor, appalled, announced that she was a naughty child and ought to pray to be given a new heart.

Mrs Reed took the opportunity to tell him in a low voice that Jane had a tendency to deceit, a fault which she hoped his teachers would watch for and correct. Mr Brocklehurst declared gravely that liars were despised by Heaven and that Jane would be kept under the strictest observation at Lowood. Jane listened to this slander in miserable silence, knowing that no one in that room would believe a word she said.

As soon as the visitor had left, something in Jane gave way, and she turned on her aunt with a boldness she had never known before. She declared that she was not deceitful, that Mrs Reed was the cruel one, and that she would tell the whole world how she had been treated. When her aunt could find no answer, Jane felt a rush of triumph, as if she had won a battle.

The feeling of victory did not last, and as the day faded the girl began to feel the sour taste of regret. Bessie, who found her trembling in the dusk, said that she was an odd, fierce, lonely little thing, but she spoke gently and without anger. Jane, who had never been so near to tenderness, drew a little comfort from the words and from the fire in the grate.

Long before dawn Jane was dressed and standing by the door, and Bessie, who had come to see her off, kissed her twice in the cold gate-house. She left Gateshead without a word of farewell from her aunt, for no one else in the house had troubled to wake, and the coach lamps cut a small yellow road through the dark. Never before had the child felt so entirely alone, nor so strangely light, as she did while the coach rolled away into the grey morning.

The journey seemed to go on for ever, through market towns and over bare hills, until the daylight faded and the lamps were lit once more. By the time the coach drew up at a pair of iron gates it was night, and the rain was falling in heavy sheets across the drive. A servant took her trunk, and Jane, too weary to be afraid, followed the light of her lantern along a path she could not see.

She was led through a maze of cold passages into a small room where a bright fire was burning and two ladies sat beside it. The taller of them, Miss Temple, had a clear fair face, a calm voice and a manner so gracious that Jane's stiff little heart softened at once. Tea and warm bread were put before her, and soon afterwards she was tucked into a narrow bed, where she slept more deeply than she had done for years.

The next morning a bell roused the whole school in the black cold, and Jane found that the water in the washing jugs had turned to ice. Eighty girls in brown woollen frocks and white aprons stood in lines to say their prayers, shivering in the gloom of a long, bare room. Breakfast was a bowl of porridge so badly scorched that it turned her stomach, and she understood that Lowood was going to be a place of hard lessons.

In the afternoon, sitting apart from the others beside a window, Jane noticed a thin, pale girl absorbed in a book, and she gathered the courage to ask its name. The girl, who introduced herself as Helen Burns, answered in a quiet, unhurried voice, and she explained that Lowood was a charity school which housed poor orphans like themselves. It was supported by the gifts of wealthy subscribers, she said, and it was managed by Mr Brocklehurst, the very man whom Jane had met at Gateshead.

Their teacher, Miss Scatcherd, a sharp-eyed woman with a sour temper, picked out Helen again and again for the smallest fault, until at last she struck her across the neck with a bundle of twigs for having dirty nails. Jane watched with burning cheeks, certain that the girl would cry out or answer back, but Helen merely stood still, with her eyes fixed on the floor. It was not courage as Jane understood it, yet it seemed to her a courage of a higher and stranger kind.

When they were alone Jane asked her friend how she could bear to be so ill-treated without protest, and said that in her place she would have fought. Helen answered in her gentle voice that life was far too short to be spent nursing hatred, and that the Bible taught men to return good for evil. Jane could not agree, but she could not help feeling that Helen understood something about the world that she herself had yet to learn.

The winter at Lowood was a hard one, with ice in the washing jugs, chilblains on every hand and meals that left the girls as hungry as before. On Sundays they were marched two miles to the church in the village, through snow that stiffened their wet clothes, and were obliged to eat a cold lunch of bread and meat in a freezing room. Many of the girls grew thin and ill, but they learned, as Jane did, to bear their misery in silence.

One morning the porridge was burnt so badly that nobody could eat it, and the girls, who had been cold since dawn, began to murmur against it. Miss Temple, who had tasted a spoonful herself, ordered a plentiful supply of bread and cheese to be served to the whole school, and she paid for it from her own store. It was the first act of open defiance against the housekeeping of Lowood that Jane had seen, and she loved the headmistress for it.

Not long afterwards Miss Temple invited Helen and Jane to join her in her own room, where a bright fire burned and a tray of tea and seed-cake had been laid. She spoke to them as if they were grown women, and Helen, who had always seemed so dreamy and untidy, began to talk with a brilliance that left Jane amazed. Jane sat entranced, hardly daring to eat, as the two of them spoke of ancient history, poetry and the lives of famous men.

In the weeks that followed, Jane applied herself to her lessons with a fierce devotion, and by degrees she rose from the bottom of her class to a respectable place near the top. Nothing more had been heard of Mr Brocklehurst's dreadful warning, and she allowed herself to hope that it had been forgotten, like so many of the grand remarks of grown men. In the evenings she sat beside Helen, content with such comforts as Lowood afforded.

That peace was broken one afternoon when the door opened and the tall black figure of Mr Brocklehurst strode into the schoolroom. Jane, remembering how he had spoken of her at Gateshead, lifted her slate before her face and tried to disappear behind it. Her hand shook so badly that it slipped, and the slate fell to the floor and broke in two with a crack that echoed through the silent room.

Mr Brocklehurst did not notice at first, for he had come with a grievance of his own, and he turned upon Miss Temple to complain about the bread and cheese she had served. The girls, he said, were being trained to endure hardship, and to feed their bodies at the expense of their souls was a fault that must not be repeated. Miss Temple heard him in a stony silence, her pale face set like marble, and never said a word in her own defence.

His eye then fell upon a pupil whose hair curled naturally round her forehead, and he demanded to know how such vanity had been allowed at Lowood. He ordered that every girl's hair should be cut close to the head, and the barber's work was begun at once. At that moment the door opened to admit his wife and daughters, who swept in wearing silks, furs and elaborate curls, and the contrast was not lost on the more observant girls.

Fixing his gaze upon Jane, the great man remembered the slate, and he called her out of her bench in a tone of cold satisfaction. She was led forward, trembling, and two teachers lifted her onto a tall stool where every pair of eyes in the room could see her. She felt that her face was burning, and that the stool, her feet and the whole floor were slowly swaying beneath her.

Mr Brocklehurst announced to the assembled school that she was an interloper in the flock of God and that a spirit of evil had already taken hold of her. She was a liar, he declared, and she was to be avoided like a plague, so that for a whole day no girl or teacher should speak to her or help her. Jane, hearing herself condemned before eighty pairs of staring eyes, felt a desolation that was greater than any she had known.

She thought she would be swallowed up in her shame, and she gripped the edge of the stool to keep herself from falling. Just then Helen Burns passed along the line with a book in her hand, and as she went by she lifted her eyes and gave Jane a smile of rare and radiant sweetness. It was like a ray of light from another world, and the girl on the stool, feeling it, straightened her back and was able to bear the rest.

When the half hour had passed and the school had been dismissed, Jane crept away into the dim corridor and flung herself on the floor, sobbing as if her heart would break. Helen found her there, knelt down beside her and held her in her thin arms, telling her that good people would never believe so foul a charge. She said that everyone who knew Jane honestly regarded her with kindness, and that God knew her innocence even if the world did not.

Later that evening Miss Temple sent for the pair of them, and she asked Jane, in a voice free of any harshness, to tell her own account of her childhood. Jane described Gateshead, the red-room and the injustice of Mrs Reed without exaggeration, and the headmistress listened with a serious attention that gave her great comfort. At the end Miss Temple promised that she would write to Mr Lloyd, whose answer would decide the matter once and for all.

A few days later the reply arrived, and it confirmed every word that Jane had spoken, adding warm praise of her character. Miss Temple, calling the school together, announced before all the pupils and teachers that Jane Eyre had been wholly cleared of every charge that had been brought against her. Jane, hardly able to believe that justice had been done, felt for the first time that Lowood might become her home.

As April warmed into May the hills around Lowood put on their green and the woods filled with flowers, yet the school itself lay at the bottom of a damp, misty hollow. The foul air and the poor food had long been preparing the way, and now a fever crept in and passed from bed to bed. Within a few weeks, half of the pupils were ill, and the lessons dwindled and stopped.

Jane, who was still strong, was allowed to roam the sunny woods all day, and she thought that she had never known such freedom. While she was so happy, a quiet sorrow was gathering, for Helen, who had suffered for a long time from a sickness of the lungs, was moved to a room of her own. Jane was told that she must not visit her, and the thought of her friend alone upstairs spoiled the pleasure of every sunny hour.

One warm evening in June, as the light lingered late over the garden, Jane learned that Helen was likely to die within days, and she could not rest. When the house had fallen silent she slipped out of her bed, wrapped herself in a shawl and crept through the dark passages to Miss Temple's room. Her heart was pounding, for she knew she would be punished if she were found, and yet nothing could have kept her away.

She found her friend lying thin and calm in a narrow bed, and Helen greeted her with a faint, loving smile and said that she had hoped she would come. She said that she was going home to God, that she was not afraid, and that she believed in a Father who would forgive everyone and keep her safe. Jane climbed in beside her, laid her head on Helen's shoulder, and sank into sleep with her friend's arms around her.

When she woke, it was daylight, and a nurse was lifting her in her arms, for Helen lay beside her, cold and quiet, having died peacefully in the night. The girl was buried in a small churchyard in the village, and for fifteen years the grave was marked only by a grassy mound. Later Jane had a grey marble tablet set up there that carried Helen's name and a single word, Resurgam.

The deaths at Lowood had been so many that the matter could not be hushed up, and a group of respected men came to inquire into the way the school was run. They found that the porridge was spoiled, the food was meagre, the building was damp and the pupils were poorly clothed, and the blame fell heavily on Mr Brocklehurst. A committee of kinder and wiser people took charge of Lowood, and a new and healthier building was soon raised on a better site.

Under its new management Lowood became in truth what it had always pretended to be, a place where poor girls could learn and grow strong. Jane flourished there, and after six years as a pupil she was made a teacher, a post she held for two more. She never lost the sense of gratitude she owed to Miss Temple, who had been her mother, her governess and her friend.

At last Miss Temple married a clergyman and left the neighbourhood, and Jane felt as though the very walls of the school had grown cold. She had lived by that lady's example for so long that the world without her seemed strangely empty and flat. As she stood at the window, her gaze travelled beyond the hills to the distant road, and she began to long for a larger and busier life.

She prayed for liberty, and then for change, and then, as no answer came, for something that the prayer could not name; at last an idea struck her, and she wrote an advertisement for the post of governess. She sent it away in secret, and, after a week of anxious waiting, an answer came in an old-fashioned hand from a Mrs Fairfax, who lived at a house called Thornfield. The terms were suitable, the situation was far from Lowood, and Jane accepted without delay.

On the eve of her departure Bessie arrived at Lowood, now Mrs Leaven and the mother of two small children, and she was delighted to see the tall, calm young woman who had once been a troubled child. She gave Jane the news of Gateshead, of the cousins and of their mother, and she added that an uncle named John Eyre had come to the house years before, asking for his niece. Jane, who had never known that she had any relative of that name, kept the thought tucked away in her mind as she set off on her journey.

After a journey that had lasted a whole day, the coach set Jane down at an inn in Millcote, in the damp and the gathering dark. She asked about a carriage from Thornfield, and the waiter replied that no one had come for her. She sat alone beside her small trunk in a strange, bare parlour, and for a moment she doubted whether she had been wise to leave the only home she had known.

After nearly an hour a stout man named John appeared with a cart, loaded her box without much ceremony, and offered no remark about the delay. They drove for ten long miles through dark lanes, past hedges that rustled in the wind and fields that were hidden in the night. Jane could see nothing but the circle of light thrown by the swinging lantern, and she told herself that the road had to lead somewhere kind.

When the cart finally stopped, Jane was led through a door and across a hall into a parlour that glowed with firelight and seemed to promise rest. A tiny, gentle old lady in a widow's cap sat knitting there, with a large cat curled at her feet, and she looked so peaceful that Jane took her at once for the mistress of the house. The lady rose, took her cold hand, and said how pleased she was that the young governess had come safely at last.

Over a late supper of tea and cold meat, the old lady explained that her name was Mrs Fairfax and that she was only the housekeeper, a distant relation of the family who had lived there for many years. The owner of Thornfield, Mr Rochester, was frequently away on his travels and was sometimes absent for months, though he had a ward whom he wished to be properly taught. Jane was relieved to learn that her employer would seldom be at home, for she had imagined a stern master who would watch over every hour of her day.

She woke the next morning to a bright sky and to a view that delighted her, for the house she had entered in darkness was old, grey and handsome. Its battlemented roof stood against a blue sky, and around it lay meadows, scattered trees and a noisy colony of rooks cawing in the elms. Jane thought that after so many years behind the walls of a charity school, she had stepped into a very pleasant place.

After breakfast she met her pupil, a small, pretty girl of about eight, who was called Adèle Varens and who spoke almost nothing but French. The child's nurse, a cheerful Frenchwoman named Sophie, was in the room as well, and Jane, who had practised the language for years at Lowood, found that she could understand them both. It was a small comfort, but it settled her nerves, and she felt that her position was beginning on the right footing.

Adèle talked incessantly about her mother, who had been an opera dancer in Paris, and she described the theatre, the lights and the beautiful dresses with great delight. She climbed on to a chair, folded her little hands and sang a song from the stage in a thin, sweet voice that was far too knowing for a child. Jane listened with a mixture of amusement and unease, and she made a silent note that the little girl had seen a good deal of the world already.

The lessons began that very morning, and Jane soon discovered that her pupil, though lively and warm-hearted, was neither clever nor disciplined and had never been taught to sit still. She was patient, however, for she remembered what it was to be a small girl with no friends, and she let kindness and routine do their work. Within a week Adèle had begun to run to her at the door, and Jane found that she was already attached to the child.

Mrs Fairfax took her through the house, from the stately dining room and the library with its tall shelves to the guest bedrooms hung with old tapestries. Everything was polished and orderly, ready to receive a crowd of visitors at a moment's notice, and yet the rooms were silent, and Jane felt that they were waiting for someone who never came. The housekeeper explained that Mr Rochester seldom visited, but that when he did, he came with guests and a great deal of noise.

At the end of the tour they climbed a narrow stair to the roof, from which Jane looked out over the fields, the hills and the little church of the village. As they came down again through the dim corridor on the third floor, with its low black doors like those of a castle, a slow, mirthless laugh sounded from one of the rooms. Jane stopped, startled, but Mrs Fairfax only said calmly that it was Grace Poole, who did the sewing up there, and she hurried the young woman on.

The first months at Thornfield passed so quietly that Jane scarcely noticed the change of the seasons, for every day followed the one before it with the regularity of a clock. She had comfort, kindness and respect, and yet in the evenings, as she walked the long corridor on the third floor with a candle in her hand, she felt that something in her was restlessly waiting for a signal. She did not know what it was, but she was sure that it was not to be found in the housekeeper's parlour.

One afternoon she climbed to the roof and stood on the battlements, gazing at the far blue hills, and wished with her whole heart that she could see more of the world and meet more of its people. She thought that women were expected to be calm, while they suffered just as men did from too narrow a life, and she told herself that it was wrong to mock them for wanting more. As she turned to go down, the same low, mirthless laugh drifted from behind the black door, and it seemed to mock her wish.

On a bitter January afternoon, when the ground rang like iron under the feet, Mrs Fairfax asked her to take a letter to the post in the village of Hay, about two miles away. Jane welcomed the errand, wrapped herself in her cloak, and set off down the lane with her bonnet tied firmly under her chin and the low sun glowing red between the bare trees. The walk was the first real outing she had taken since the autumn, and she enjoyed every step of it.

Beside the lane stood a stile, and there Jane rested for a while and watched the silent landscape fade from gold to grey. As she sat, she remembered a story Bessie used to tell her about the Gytrash, a spirit of the north that haunted lonely roads as a horse, a mule or a huge dog. The thought amused her more than it frightened her, and she told herself that she was too old for such tales.

Even so, when she heard the slow thud of hooves on the frozen ground, a shiver went through her, and she held her breath. First there trotted into view an enormous dog with a black and white coat and a long, shaggy head, which passed her with hardly a glance, as if it had seen nothing strange. Behind it came a horse with a rider on its back, and the whole group came round the bend of the lane like a picture from an old story.

The horse, a tall, dark animal, set its foot on a sheet of ice that lay hidden in the ruts, and its legs went out from under it in a sudden scramble. The rider was flung out of the saddle and landed heavily on the frozen road, while the dog, which seemed to understand that something was wrong, began to bark with a deep, ringing voice. The sound rolled over the empty fields, and it seemed to Jane that all the hills were answering.

She ran to him at once, asking whether he was badly hurt, and the stranger answered her with a muttered curse and a few words that were not meant to be polite. He had sprained his ankle, as it turned out, and he leaned upon her shoulder with a weight that she felt right to the bone as he limped across to the horse. It was not a gentle way of accepting help, but Jane did not think it unkind, and she held his arm until he was steady.

Now that he was upright, she saw that he was a dark, broad man of about thirty-five, with a stern face, a square jaw and thick black brows drawn together in pain. He was dressed like a gentleman, in a fur-collared coat, but she thought that he was not handsome, and she felt no fear of him whatever. He asked her whom she lived with and what she did, and when she answered that she was governess at Thornfield Hall, he looked at her for a long moment and said nothing.

Despite his sprain, he climbed back into the saddle with a hard, set face, thanked her shortly, and rode away with the dog bounding at his side. Jane stood for a moment in the empty lane, then walked on to the village and dropped her letter in the box, and the whole way home she thought about the episode. It was a very small event, but it had stirred her quiet life like a stone thrown into a still pond, and she did not want to go back to a pond without ripples.

When she reached Thornfield, the moon was high, and a strange gig was waiting in the drive, while a man in the hall was speaking in low tones with the surgeon, Mr Carter. Mrs Fairfax came out to meet her, saying that the master had arrived unexpectedly, that his horse had slipped on the ice at Hay Lane, and that he had sprained his ankle badly. Jane understood at once who the dark stranger was, and she felt a small, strange thrill of embarrassment and curiosity.

That evening, Jane took Adèle down to the dining room, where the lamps were lit and a great fire roared in the grate. The master of Thornfield lay on a couch with his bandaged foot raised on a cushion and the enormous dog Pilot stretched out beside him, and he did not raise his eyes when the governess and her pupil entered. Jane waited at the door, uncertain, aware that a man who was so little polite could not expect her to be shy.

Adèle had been questioning everyone all day about the gifts that he had promised her, and when her box was brought in, she hugged it with a cry of joy. Mr Rochester let her have her pleasure, and then he turned his dark, heavy face toward Jane and told her curtly to draw her chair closer to the fire. She obeyed, folding her hands in her lap, and bore his steady gaze without lowering her own.

He asked in a quick, abrupt manner about her family, about the school at Lowood and about the years she had spent there, and she answered as briefly as the questions allowed. Then, with the same hard stare and no hint of a smile, he asked her whether she found him handsome. Jane, who had never learned the art of the flattering reply, felt the question land like a dart in a target.

Without any thought of the consequences, she answered that she did not, and the words were out before she could think better of them. To her surprise the master threw back his head and laughed, not in anger but with a kind of delighted astonishment, and he declared that she had the manner of a child, yet not the mind of one. It was clear that such honesty was a rare thing in his house, and that he valued it more than he said.

He told her to go to the piano and play something, and she chose two simple pieces that she had practised at Lowood. He listened with his head bent and his eyes half closed, then raised a hand and said that this would do, since she played like a schoolgirl, neatly and without much fire. Jane took no offence, for she knew that the judgement was fair, and she thought that his candour was easier to bear than praise that she did not deserve.

Next he asked to see the paintings that she had mentioned, and she brought him three watercolours from her portfolio, which he spread on the table beside the lamp. He studied each of them in silence for a long time, holding one to the light and frowning, and then asked where in the world she had found such strange visions. They showed a stormy sea, a woman's face among the clouds, and an evening star above a black hill, and they were certainly not what a governess was supposed to paint.

She replied that the pictures had come out of her own head, and that she had made them in the happiest hours of her life at Lowood. He answered, with a small, grim smile, that he had thought so, and that they were the work of an unquiet mind. Then he glanced at the clock, observed that the child was nodding on her feet, and dismissed both of them to bed with a wave of his hand.

Mrs Fairfax told her afterwards that the master was a man of changing moods, who had endured a number of troubles within his family and was therefore seldom at peace under his own roof. Jane considered the matter for some time, and she concluded that she could bear his abruptness well enough, since his roughness was open and honest and had no hypocrisy in it. She found that she preferred a master who said what he thought to one who covered his meaning with sweet words.

On the following evenings he sent for her again and sat talking with her by the fire, while Pilot dozed on the rug and Adèle played in a corner with her new doll. At last, in a voice that was low and bitter, he told her the story of Céline Varens, the Parisian dancer whom he had once loved and who had deceived him with a young officer while pretending to adore him. When she left the city, Adèle was left behind, and he had taken the child away.

He did not believe that the little girl was his daughter, he said, but he could not leave her to the streets of Paris, so he had brought her to England. Jane, listening, saw that the harsh and hasty man had a kinder heart than he cared to admit, and that his anger was only the hard shell of an old wound. When she went upstairs that night and looked at the sleeping child, she felt a sudden warm rush of tenderness for them both.

As the winter deepened, Jane came to know the master's moods the way a sailor knows the sky. One day he would pass her in the hall without so much as a nod, and on the next he would stop and talk with her for an hour, as freely as if they were old friends. She could not tell why, but with her he seemed to lay down a heavy burden, and she found herself looking forward to his coming with a pleasure that she took care not to examine.

One night she woke from a light sleep with the unmistakable feeling that something had passed close to her door. There was a murmur like the fumbling of a hand upon the wood, and then, low and slow and altogether wicked, a laugh that seemed to freeze the very air of the passage. Footsteps shuffled away toward the third-floor stair, and she lay quite still, with her heart thudding in her ears.

At last she rose, wrapped herself in a shawl and opened the door, and there at her feet, on the matting, a candle was burning. The corridor beyond was thick with smoke, a grey and choking cloud that wound out from under the door of Mr Rochester's chamber. Without stopping to think what she was doing, she ran to the door and pushed it open.

Within, the bed curtains were blazing, and the flames were already licking up the canopy and spreading over the sheets in long, hungry tongues. In the middle of the fire, stretched out on his back, lay Mr Rochester, sunk in a heavy and unnatural sleep, with the smoke rolling over his face. Jane cried out his name, but he neither stirred nor answered, and she knew that there was not a moment to lose.

She shook him as hard as she could and, finding that he did not wake, flew to the washstand and seized the basin and the large jug that stood beside it. She emptied both over the bed and the sleeper, and the water put out the fire with a roar of steam and a smell of scorched wood. By the time she had run for more, the room had fallen black and silent, and the master was sitting up and swearing.

He asked, between oaths, what in the world had happened, and when Jane had told him in a few quick sentences, he put on a coat and gave her a look of strange, alert gravity. He told her to wait for him where she stood and not to wake a soul, and then he took the candle and strode away toward the stairs to the third floor. She stood shivering in the darkness, soaked to the skin, and counted every minute of his absence.

When the light of his candle came back down the stairs, it was a long time since he had left, and his face was set and pale. He said that it was exactly as he had feared, that Grace Poole was responsible, and that he would deal with it himself, and he made her promise to tell no one. Jane agreed, though she could not stop herself from wondering at a master who was so gentle with a servant who had tried to burn him alive.

Then, in a voice that was quite different from his usual tones, he thanked her for saving his life, and said that he knew he owed her a debt he could never fully repay. He took her hand and held it for a moment, much longer than he needed to, and she felt the pressure of it long after she had gone. She went back to her cold bed with her mind in a tumult, and it was a long time before she slept.

She rose early and tired, and the first thing she learned was that Mr Rochester had left Thornfield at dawn, without a word to anyone. When she looked into his bedroom, she found it blackened and wet and filled with the smell of the fire, and there, in the grey morning light, sat Grace Poole by the window, calmly stitching a new curtain. The woman looked up with a quiet, steady face, and nothing in her manner suggested that anything in the world had gone amiss.

Jane watched the large, plain, middle-aged face for a sign of fear or guilt, and she watched in vain. Grace merely remarked that her master ought to know better than to sleep with a candle burning, and then she bent again over her work as if the subject were closed. Jane left the room with a head full of questions, wondering how a woman who had set a house on fire could be so calm, and why Mr Rochester had let her stay.

Mr Rochester had been gone for a fortnight, and then for longer, and Thornfield seemed to Jane to have lost its colour, like a room from which the lamp has been taken away. She told herself that she had no reason to miss him, since he was her master and she a servant, but the thought brought her little comfort. The house was quiet and tidy and kind, and yet in every corridor she felt the want of one particular footstep.

At last Mrs Fairfax let slip that he was staying at a large country house, where a gay party had gathered and Miss Blanche Ingram was thought to be the chief attraction. The housekeeper described her as a tall, dark, regal young woman of great accomplishment and fortune, who would suit Mr Rochester well in rank and in wealth. She added, with a significant glance, that it would be no surprise if she came to Thornfield as its mistress.

Jane felt a pang so sharp and so foolish that it startled her, and she resolved at once to punish herself for it. She took a piece of chalk and a sheet of paper and drew, with unsparing honesty, a portrait of her own face, with its thin cheeks, pale skin and small, plain features. Underneath she wrote the words Governess, Orphan, Penniless and Plain, and she looked at them with a stern calm.

Then she took her best colours and a small ivory panel and painted, as carefully as she could, a picture of the imagined Miss Ingram, with dark ringlets, flashing eyes and a proud, lovely mouth. When it was done, she set the splendid miniature beside the chalk drawing and studied the two together, so that she might never again forget the difference between them. It was a stern lesson, and she told herself that she would repeat it every day until it had been learned.

Within a few days Mrs Fairfax announced that the master was returning on the Thursday, bringing with him a large company that was to stay for several weeks. The house became a bustle of servants, sheets and flowers, and when the carriages came up the drive at last, Jane watched from the gallery above the hall. Ladies in riding habits and gentlemen in great coats descended in a cloud of laughter, and the quiet old house suddenly became a stage.

That evening Mr Rochester sent a message that Jane and Adèle were to come down and be introduced to the company, and Jane, who would have much preferred to remain upstairs, put on her only good dress and obeyed. She found a seat in a window recess half hidden by a curtain, and set a book before her face, so that she could study the scene without being observed in her turn. The room was dazzling with candlelight, silk and jewels, and she felt like a small grey bird among peacocks.

The ladies sat in a graceful half-circle, and they talked about everything that occurred to them with the careless confidence of people who had never been poor. Lady Ingram, a stately matron, declared that governesses were an unbearable plague, and the other ladies laughed and added their own stories of the stupidity and the pretension of such persons. Jane, who was sitting not ten feet away, turned a page of her book with a steady hand and made no sign that she had heard.

Presently Blanche Ingram went to the grand piano and sang in a rich, strong, confident voice, and the master stood beside her with his arm resting easily on the instrument. The guests applauded loudly, and Mr Rochester looked down at the singer with an expression that Jane could not read, but that stabbed her all the same. She put down her book, rose without a word and slipped out of the room before anyone had time to notice her go.

She had almost reached the foot of the stairs when she heard a quick step behind her, and Mr Rochester came out into the hall and caught her by the hand under the hanging lamp. He asked, with a hint of impatience, why she had not wished him good evening, and why she was leaving before the party was over. She answered quietly that she had not wished to disturb him, and that she was a little tired, and he let her go with a curious look.

In her room Jane stood at the window with her forehead against the cold glass, looking down at the dark garden, and she let herself at last say the truth. She loved the master of Thornfield, who was rich and clever and quite out of her reach, and who was probably going to marry another woman within the month. It was a hard and humbling thing to know, and she resolved there and then that nobody, least of all he, should ever discover it.

Mr Rochester had ridden to Millcote on business, and without him the house party fell into a lazy and slightly peevish mood, for the guests had grown used to being amused by their host. Late in the afternoon a servant announced with an air of mystery that an old gypsy woman was at the door, demanding to be allowed in. She wanted nothing, she said, but to tell the fortunes of the ladies of the house.

She was shown into the library, and the young ladies went in to see her one at a time, each coming out with a different face. Some of them returned laughing and flushed, while others, among them Miss Ingram, came back thoughtful and silent, and none would repeat a word of what had been said. The suspense among the gentlemen grew greater with each lady that returned, and at last it was Jane's turn.

A message arrived that the old woman had asked for the governess too, and Jane, who had no wish to be the last, nevertheless walked into the library and took a chair on the far side of the fire. The gypsy was bent over the grate in a red cloak and a broad black hat, with a bandage under her chin, and her face was almost hidden. Jane told her in a steady voice that she did not believe in fortune-telling, and that she wanted nothing from it.

The old woman peered at her face, studied her palm in the firelight and said in a low, rough voice that she was cold, sick and silly, for she would not accept the warmth within her reach. She added that Jane had a secret hope, one that was hidden even from herself, and that happiness was close beside her if only she would stretch out a hand. Jane smiled, shook her head and answered each question with so much care that the gypsy grew impatient.

While she was speaking, however, Jane noticed the shape of the hand on the fire-iron and heard a certain tone in the voice that she knew too well to be wrong. She looked at the cloak, and at the long fingers, and she understood the truth a moment before the old woman threw off the hat and the bandage. There, laughing at his own cleverness, sat Mr Rochester, who had come back a quarter of an hour before and decided to try his guests.

That evening, as the household was still laughing over the joke, a stranger arrived at Thornfield, a tall, pale gentleman with a gentle, weak face, who said that his name was Mr Mason and that he had come from Jamaica. Mr Rochester, who had been in high spirits, went suddenly grey when he heard the name, and for an instant Jane saw him stagger as though struck. He recovered himself at once, welcomed the guest with a forced and hearty air, and led him in to supper.

At midnight, when the house was quiet and the candles had been put out, a terrible cry rang out from the third floor, a wild and piercing call for help. Doors opened, the guests ran out onto the landing in their nightclothes, and Lady Ingram fell into a fit of weeping, while the gentlemen demanded to know what was wrong. Mr Rochester appeared among them with perfect calm, declared that a servant had had a nightmare, and so persuaded them, with some difficulty, to go back to their rooms.

A little later he found Jane waiting dressed in the passage, and he asked her in a low voice to bring a sponge and some water and to make no noise. He took a candle and led her up the narrow stair to the third floor, where he unlocked a small door and showed her into a dim chamber. On the bed, with his shirt stained red and his head thrown back, lay Mr Mason, who was bleeding heavily from the arm and shoulder.

Mr Rochester told her that he must fetch the surgeon, and that she was to keep the wounded man quiet and was not, on any account, to let him talk. Then he left her alone with the candle and the stricken guest, and she heard the door of the next room tremble as something moved behind it with a sound like a low, savage snarl. For two long hours she sponged the wound, listening to the quiet of the house and the movement behind the wall, and never once did she turn her head.

Dawn was breaking when Mr Carter, the surgeon, arrived with Mr Rochester, and he dressed the injury with a look of grave surprise, murmuring that it looked very much as if the man had been bitten. Before any of the guests had woken, Mr Rochester helped the wounded man into a carriage and sent him away into the grey morning, with the promise that he would be properly cared for. Jane stood at the window and watched it go, certain that she had seen a part of a secret that she was not yet allowed to know.

At sunrise the next morning, when the guests were still asleep, Mr Rochester walked with Jane through the damp garden, among the roses and the dew-soaked grass. He asked her, in a thoughtful and almost troubled voice, how she would judge a man who had made a grave mistake when he was young and had suffered for it ever since. He wanted to know whether such a man might ever hope to begin again.

Jane considered the question with her usual seriousness and replied that she would feel only pity for such a man, and that she believed no mistake could cancel the possibility of goodness. Mr Rochester listened with his eyes on the ground and then said, rather quietly, that her answer gave him a comfort she could not guess. She did not understand what he meant, but she held the words in her memory as one holds a stone that may later prove to be precious.

A few days later, as the guests were beginning to talk of leaving, a man in a black coat came to the gate and asked for Miss Eyre, and Jane recognised him as Robert Leaven, the Gateshead coachman. He had ridden a long way in the heat, and his face, which was usually kind, was grave with the news that he carried. He stood with his hat in his hand and waited for her to read the letter that he gave her.

John Reed, he told her, had lived so wildly that he had ruined his name and his fortune, and he was now dead, to the great grief and shame of his family. His mother had been so shocked by the news that she had suffered a stroke, and since then she had lain speechless for days, murmuring only the name of Jane. The household hoped, he said, that Miss Eyre would come, if she could be spared.

Jane went to find Mr Rochester in the library and told him plainly that she must go to see her aunt, who was ill and had asked for her. He answered with a joke about her running away to a better situation, but when she assured him that she meant to return, he gave her leave and asked how long she would need. His eyes followed her with an expression that she could not decipher as she left the room.

That evening she packed her small trunk with her plain dresses, while Adèle sat on the bed and asked a hundred questions about the journey and about the aunt. Mr Rochester, who came to the door of her room for a moment to say goodbye, told her in a grave voice that he would expect her to come back, and that she was not to stay away. Jane promised him that she would return, though the promise cost her more than she cared to show.

Early the next morning she took the coach, which rolled all day along wide white roads and through fields that were ripe for the harvest. She felt oddly dreamlike as she travelled, for she was going back to the house that she had left at ten years old as an unloved and angry child, and she had no idea what she would find there. By evening the familiar hills of the north had come into view, and her heart began to beat faster.

At the lodge gate a stout woman in a bonnet was waiting, with her hands clasped before her, and Jane recognised Bessie, who ran to her and kissed her on both cheeks. They talked all the way up the long drive, each asking and answering a dozen questions at once, and it seemed to Jane that she had never in her life been so warmly and simply welcomed. For the first time she thought that perhaps she had a place in the world after all.

In the drawing room, the two cousins were sitting in black dresses at a table covered with sewing, one tall and pale and stern, the other fair and pretty and listless. Eliza gave Jane a quick glance and a cold word of greeting, and Georgiana held out two fingers and asked whether the journey had been dusty. Jane saw that they had not changed much in eight years, and she sat down among them as quietly as a stranger.

Mrs Reed lay propped against the pillows in the great bedroom, with her face thin and hardened by illness and her eyes as sharp and bright as ever. She looked at the tall young woman who stood at the foot of her bed and asked in a weak but firm voice whether this was really Jane Eyre. Jane answered that it was, and she took the old woman's hand in hers, though it did not return the pressure.

Jane stayed on at Gateshead for nearly a month, while her aunt sank slowly toward the end of her illness. Georgiana lay on a sofa complaining of the dullness of the country, and Eliza, who kept strictly to a plan of work and prayer, did not trouble to visit the sickroom. Neither of them seemed to feel the sorrow that the house was waiting to receive.

One night, when the room was silent and the fire had burned low, Mrs Reed beckoned to Jane with a thin hand and told her to come closer to the bed. She said, in a voice that was low and hoarse with illness, that she had done Jane a wrong, and that she could not die until she had spoken of it. Jane waited, with her heart beating fast, to hear what the old woman had hidden for so long.

Three years before, said Mrs Reed, a letter had come from a gentleman named John Eyre, who was Jane's uncle and who was living in Madeira as a wine merchant. He had written that he was rich and childless, and that he wished to adopt his niece and leave her his fortune, and he had asked where she might be found. Mrs Reed had written back that Jane had died of fever at Lowood, and she had kept the matter secret.

She confessed with a trembling mouth that she had never been able to forgive Jane for being her husband's favourite, because he had loved the orphan more tenderly than his own children. As though that were her last act of honesty, she asked Jane to open the drawer of her desk, and from it she took out the letter, which was crumpled and yellow. Jane held it in her hand and could hardly believe the date it bore.

In that hour Jane felt every old grievance fall away, and she told her aunt, with tears in her eyes, that she forgave her fully and freely, and asked for forgiveness in return. Mrs Reed looked at her with the old coldness for a moment, then turned her face to the wall and said that Jane had a wicked disposition and that she had always disliked her. Jane saw that it was too late to change a heart that had been hardened for so many years.

Before dawn Mrs Reed died, quite alone in the dark, and Jane sat beside her through the last hours with a candle burning on the table. She felt no triumph at all, only a quiet and complicated pity for the woman who had been so unhappy and who had made so many others unhappy too. The room was very still, and she looked at the stiff, set face and thought how little hatred had ever profited anyone.

After the funeral, when the black carriages had come back from the village and the mourners had drunk their tea in silence, Eliza told Jane that she meant to enter a convent in France. She spoke with perfect calm, as one who had planned her whole life in advance, and she showed Jane her desk with its neat piles of papers and the keys on a ring. She had arranged everything, even the sale of the house, and no one was to argue with her.

Georgiana, who was as fair and as foolish as ever, announced that she would go to London to be presented in society and make a brilliant marriage with a rich man. The two sisters took leave of each other with hardly a kiss or a tear, and Jane saw that they had never really cared for one another and would seldom meet again. She was sorry for it, but she also knew that nothing she could do would change them.

At last Jane was free to go, and she left Gateshead by the coach with an odd lightness, as if a stone had been taken from her chest. All the long road she thought of Thornfield and of the person who waited there, and she wondered whether the master had married Miss Ingram while she was away. It was a thought she had tried for a month to ignore, and now it came back with a force that made her hands tremble.

She left the coach at Millcote on a warm midsummer evening and chose to walk the last two miles across the fields, because she wished to arrive slowly and to compose herself. The hay lay in long rows in the meadows, the air was sweet and golden, and the sky was full of the last light of the day. At the stile by the gate, with a sketchbook on his knee, a dark-cloaked man was sitting, and Jane stopped at once.

Mr Rochester sprang up from the stile when he saw her, took both of her hands in his and said that he had known she would come back, since he had so often seen her in his dreams. He told her, with a sort of happy roughness, that Thornfield had been empty without her, and that she had been a long time away. Jane felt the blood rush to her face, and she looked at the grass so that he would not see how much the words had moved her.

At the house, Mrs Fairfax and Adèle ran out to greet her, and the old housekeeper kissed her on both cheeks, while the little girl danced around her skirts, shouting in French. Jane felt as if she had been in a long cold exile and had come home at last, and for several days she was very happy. She took care, however, not to think too closely about the wedding that was sure to be coming, or about what it would mean for her.

One warm evening, when the sun had gone down and the first stars were beginning to show, Jane was walking alone in the orchard, and Mr Rochester came across the grass to join her. He spoke at first about small things, and then, with an effort, he told her that he was to be married very soon, and that she and Adèle would be obliged to leave. Jane felt a chill pass through her, although the summer air was warm and still.

He said that he had heard of a good situation for her in Ireland, in the house of a lady named Mrs O'Gall, who had five daughters and lived at a place called Bitternut Lodge. He said, with a kind of bitter gentleness, that it was a long way off and that a wide sea would lie between them, and that they would probably never meet again. Jane stood still, for it seemed to her that the world had come to an end.

She stopped beneath the great chestnut tree and put out her hand against its trunk, and tears ran down her cheeks and fell on the grass. She tried to say that she would be sorry to leave Thornfield, which she loved as her own home, but her voice broke, and she could not hide that her grief was for a much greater loss. The thought of the master married to another woman and living far from her was more than she could bear.

At last she cried out, in a voice that shook with passion, that she was not a machine without feelings, nor a bird caught in a net, but a free human being with an independent will. She told him that if God had given her beauty and wealth, it would have been as hard for him to leave her as it was now for her to leave him, since in spirit they stood equal before God. When she had finished speaking, she stood trembling from head to foot beneath the dark branches.

Rochester took both her hands in the twilight and said, in a low and urgent voice, that his bride was beside him, and that it was Jane whom he meant to marry. Jane, who had heard nothing of the kind in all her days, turned away in anger, thinking that he was mocking her, and she begged him not to be so cruel. He swore with every solemn word he knew that he loved her, and that he was in earnest.

She told him that it was unkind to joke, that Miss Ingram would never allow it, and that she was a poor, plain and obscure creature, while the lady was a great beauty. He answered with contempt that Blanche Ingram cared only for his money and that he had pretended to court her merely to see whether Jane would be jealous. He said that Jane herself was the only one who had touched his heart in years.

Jane looked into his face, which was pale and trembling in the dusk, and she saw that every feature was alive with honest and passionate feeling. All her doubts melted like frost in the sun, and she said, simply and gravely, that she would be his wife, and that she would be proud to be so. He drew her close to him and held her, and for a few moments the whole garden seemed filled with song.

While they stood together under the great tree, the wind began to rise, a distant roll of thunder sounded over the hills, and the first heavy drops of rain fell on their faces. They ran laughing for the house, and as they reached the door a blinding flash of lightning struck the old chestnut tree, and with a tremendous crack it split down the middle. The two halves hung apart in the darkness, one of them black and ruined, and the other still standing.

In the weeks that followed, Mr Rochester took Jane to Millcote and bought her silks, jewels and a long veil of the finest lace, with the delight of a man who has waited many years for someone to spoil. Jane, who had never had more than a single plain dress, felt like a doll being dressed for show, and she begged him in a low voice to stop. He only said that he enjoyed it, and she was left to endure the gifts with a smile.

That night she wrote to her uncle, John Eyre, in Madeira, telling him of her aunt's confession, of her own safety and of her coming marriage to Mr Rochester. She hoped, she said, that he might leave her a small sum of money, because she disliked the thought of being a penniless bride dependent on her husband's generosity. She sealed the letter and sent it away with great care, as though it held a part of her future.

Mrs Fairfax drew her aside one afternoon, with a troubled face, and said gently that she must be careful, for a master and a governess were not equals. She added that gentlemen often changed their minds before they had been married a year, and that she hoped Jane would not be hurt. Jane thanked her warmly, but she was too happy to feel anything but gratitude for the good woman's concern.

Mr Rochester, in the meantime, grew a little too proud of his own generosity, and Jane took every chance to tease him and bring him back to earth. She told him that she would not become a grand lady, that she would remain simply herself and that he must not expect her to wear all of the jewels at once. He laughed aloud and said that he loved her all the better for her sauciness, and that no one could ever change her.

The wedding was fixed for a month later, and on the night before it, Mr Rochester was called away to Millcote on some pressing business. A wild wind began to blow around Thornfield, the rain beat on the windows and the old trees moaned in the dark, and Jane, in spite of all that was ready for the morning, could not sleep. She wandered about her room, looking at the white dress and the veil that hung on the wardrobe door.

A little after midnight, as she lay with open eyes, the door opened without a sound, and a tall, dark woman came in with a candle in her hand. She was not Mrs Fairfax or Leah or Grace Poole, for Jane had never seen her face, and yet there was something horribly familiar about the way she moved. Without a word the stranger took the wedding veil from its hook, held it up in the light and set it upon her own head.

In the mirror Jane saw her reflection, a wild, savage face, discoloured and red, with fierce eyes and long, tangled black hair that fell over her shoulders. The woman looked at the veil for a moment, then took it from her head, tore it from the top to the bottom, flung the pieces on the floor and trampled them. Then she bent over the bed with her candle, held it close to Jane's face, and the girl fainted.

When Jane woke it was already day, and Mr Rochester was sitting at her bedside, holding her hand and looking pale. He listened to her story with a serious face and said that part of it was a dream, but that the torn veil was real, and that it had been the work of Grace Poole. He begged her to be patient and promised that, in a year and a day, he would explain everything.

On the wedding morning Jane put on a simple white dress, because she wished to be as plain and honest as she could, and she and Mr Rochester set off on foot for the little church, which stood close by. The house had been closed up, Mrs Fairfax and Adèle stood and watched from the door, and no one else had been invited. Jane felt very nervous, but she held Mr Rochester's arm and walked with her head up.

In the little church, the vicar read the service in a slow, solemn voice, and then he asked whether anyone knew of a lawful reason why the two should not be joined. For a moment there was complete silence, and then a clear voice sounded from the back of the church. A man in a dark coat had risen from his pew and was walking calmly up the aisle.

The man in the dark coat was Mr Briggs, a London lawyer, and he declared in a calm, clear voice that the marriage could not proceed, because Mr Rochester already had a wife who was still living. He read from a paper that the gentleman had married Bertha Antoinette Mason fifteen years before in the island of Jamaica, and that the lady, as far as he knew, was at present living at Thornfield Hall. The whole church seemed to turn to stone as the dreadful words fell upon the silent air and the listeners.

Mr Rochester did not deny it, and his face grew hard and dark, like a rock under a thundercloud. He told the vicar sharply to close the book, because the ceremony was at an end, and then he asked all of them to follow him to the house. His voice shook with a suppressed fury that Jane had never heard before, and she trembled to hear it.

At the side of the lawyer a pale, gentle-faced man stepped forward, and Jane recognised Mr Mason, the stranger who had been wounded in the night at Thornfield. He explained quietly that the Bertha in question was his own sister, that she was alive and living in the house and that he himself had seen her there only a few weeks before. He added that he had heard of the intended marriage from a gentleman in Madeira, who was Jane's own uncle, and that he had come at once with the lawyer.

Mr Rochester led the whole party back to the house and up the stairs, past the bedrooms and the empty drawing rooms to the third floor, where the corridor was low and dark. At the end of the passage he lifted an old tapestry that hung from the wall and unlocked a small black door, and he held up a lamp so that all could see inside. Jane followed with the rest, and her heart was beating so hard that she could scarcely breathe.

The room beyond had no window, and it was lit only by a fire in the grate, behind a high guard, where Grace Poole sat quietly stirring something in a pan. In the shadows at the other end, something large and dark was moving backward and forward on all fours, snarling like a wild animal, with a long grey mane that hid its head. It was only when it stood upright that the visitors saw it was a woman.

The figure sprang up with a wild cry, rushed at Mr Rochester, who was a strong man, and seized him by the throat, and for several minutes they fought in silence while the watchers stood frozen. At last, with all his strength, he caught her arms, forced her down into a chair and bound her fast with cords, though she snarled and struggled against them. When it was done, he stood up, breathing hard and streaked with sweat, and he looked at the company with burning eyes.

He turned to the shocked company, white as paper, and said in a low, bitter voice that this was his wife, the woman to whom he had been bound for fifteen years. No one answered him, and the gentlemen and the lawyer went quietly down the stairs. Jane walked to her own room in a trance, shut the door, locked it and sat down on the bed.

Later in the day Mr Rochester came to her door and begged her to let him in, and at last, feeling that she must hear him out, she opened it. He told her the whole story, how his father and brother had arranged a marriage with Bertha Mason for her fortune, and how within four years she had shown signs of terrible madness. Her family had hidden the truth from him until it was far too late to undo what had been done.

He had brought her to Thornfield, he said, and had placed her in the care of Grace Poole, since he could not bear the thought of sending his wife to an asylum, however mad she might be. Then he took Jane's hands, begged her to leave England with him and live with him as his wife in the south of France, and said that nothing could be a sin that harmed no one. His voice trembled with the force of his pleading, and his eyes never left her face for a moment.

Jane wept, but she did not waver, and she told him that she could not do it, however much she loved him, for such laws were not made for times when there was no temptation. She cared for herself, she said, and the more solitary and friendless she was, the more she must respect herself, and she would keep the principles that she had held when she was sane. When he had gone, she lay awake and decided that she must leave Thornfield before the morning.

Before it was light, Jane rose, dressed in the dark and made up a small bundle of linen, taking with her the twenty shillings that she had in her purse. She went to the little bed where Adèle lay asleep and kissed her gently on the forehead, and then she looked once more at her own pale face in the glass. It was the last time she would ever see herself in that quiet room, and the thought made her catch her breath.

She crept along the passage in her stockings, with her shoes in her hand, and as she passed Mr Rochester's door she thought she could hear him breathing, and her heart almost failed. She forced herself on, down the stairs and through the kitchen, and a moment later she was outside, on the cold wet grass, with the grey morning in front of her. She did not look back at the dark house, because she knew that if she did, she would never be able to leave.

She hurried for two miles through the fields to a crossroads where the coach stopped, and she took the first one that came, as it happened to be going north. She handed the driver all that she had, which was every shilling in her purse, and she did not even ask where he was going. Her one wish was to be as far from Thornfield as money could carry her, and the money ended there.

Two days later, in the evening, the coach set her down at a place called Whitcross, which was nothing but a signpost where four roads met on a lonely moor. She looked in vain for a village, for a house, or for a person, and when she put her hand to her side, she discovered that she had left her bundle in the coach. It was her last possession in the world, and now it was gone, and she stood alone on the empty road with nothing at all.

She had no money, no food and no one to turn to, but she walked out across the great moor, which was purple with heather and quiet in the dying light. She found a hollow among the stones and sank into the thick heather, and she lay there looking up at the stars while the tears ran silently down her face. After a long time, sleep came to her, and she was grateful for it.

In the morning she walked on until she found a village, and there she tried to sell her handkerchief and her gloves for a little food, but no one wanted them. The baker, who looked at her with an air of suspicion, said that he had nothing for beggars, and a shopkeeper told her that she should go to the parish. She came away with the feeling that the world had no room for a poor and homeless woman.

At a lonely farm, she offered to work for a little bread, but the farmer's wife only shook her head, since she had no use for a stranger. Another woman, who had been standing at the door, took pity on her, and gave her a thick slice of bread, which Jane ate by the roadside. She thought that no feast had ever tasted so sweet, and she wept to think of such kindness.

That night it began to rain, and Jane crept into a wet wood and lay down under the branches, as cold and as wretched as she had ever been. She was so weak and so hungry that she thought she might not wake again, and in a strange way she did not mind, for she felt that God was near. She said her prayers, wrapped her wet shawl about her and closed her eyes.

On the third night, as she dragged herself along a stony path, she saw in the distance a small yellow light, shining low across the dark marsh. She got up and walked toward it, falling many times, and at every fall she thought that she could go no farther, yet she went on. It took her hours to cross the wet and treacherous ground, but the light stayed in her sight.

At last she came to a house, low and old, standing alone with its windows glowing, and she knocked at the door with her last strength. An old servant opened it a little way, looked at the thin, pale, ragged creature in the rain and said that she could not take in beggars, and she shut the door. Jane sank down upon the cold step, with the rain beating on her bare head, believing that this was the end.

A quiet voice behind her said that she must not die on that step, and a tall young man bent down, gathered her up in his arms and carried her through the door. He was St John Rivers, the clergyman of the village of Morton, who had come home that evening from his work, and he took her into the warm and lamplit kitchen. Jane, almost fainting, felt that she had been brought back from the edge of the grave.

His sisters, Diana and Mary, gave her small pieces of bread and milk and warm covers, and they spoke to her as if she were their own. When they asked her name, she said that it was Jane Elliott, for she was afraid that Mr Rochester might somehow find her, and she did not want to bring shame on the people who had saved her. She added that she had no friends and no home, and the sisters did not press her to say more.

For three days Jane lay in bed in a small, clean room, so weak that she could hardly lift her head, and the sisters came to look after her. On the fourth day the old servant Hannah came to the bedside, and she said that she was sorry she had turned a poor girl from the door, and that she had never known such a night. Jane smiled and told her that no one could blame her, and the old woman went away consoled.

As her strength returned, Jane found that she had fallen among people of rare intelligence and gentle manners, though they were poor and their home was plain. The two sisters, who were dark and quick and fond of reading, had been governesses in the south, and they had come home to bury their father, who had died only a few weeks before. Their small inheritance had gone, and they would soon have to go back to work in the houses of strangers.

In the long evenings, while the wind blew over the moor, Diana and Mary taught Jane German, and Jane read their books and listened to their talk with great pleasure. She came to love them with all her heart, and she felt that she was no longer an outcast. Their brother, St John, sat apart, reading or writing in his study, with a stern, handsome face like a statue, and he said very little to anyone.

One day St John called Jane into the study and asked her quietly what she could do and what work she would take, since she could not live on charity for ever. When she answered that she would do any honest work, he told her that a school for poor girls was about to open in the village of Morton, and he offered her the post of its teacher. It was a humble place, he warned, but Jane did not hesitate to accept.

He found her a small cottage near the school, which had two rooms, a bed, a table and two chairs, and was lit by a window that looked over the green fields. A young orphan named Alice was to help her with the housework, and Jane, who had been so poor for so long, thought it the finest house she had ever seen. She settled in with the quiet delight of someone who has found a safe harbour.

On the first morning thirty poor village girls came to the schoolroom in clogs and patched shawls, and they were rough and slow, and a good many could not read a word. Jane worked hard to teach them, but at the end of the day she sat alone and felt that she had come down very far from the great rooms of Thornfield. She wiped her tears and told herself that she must be content with her honest bread.

One afternoon a lovely young woman in a bright bonnet and a silk dress came into the schoolroom, and Jane learned that she was Rosamond Oliver, the daughter of the richest man in the district. She was as kind as she was beautiful, and she brought gifts and sweets to the pupils, and the poor girls gazed at her as if she were an angel come down from heaven. Jane, who had never seen anyone so graceful, was charmed by her gentle manners and her ready laughter.

Jane soon observed that St John could scarcely keep his eyes off Rosamond whenever she was near, and that he loved her with a hidden and painful passion. But he told Jane that he would never marry her, because he intended to go as a missionary to India, and a delicate young woman like Rosamond would never survive the life that he planned. She saw that he fought his feelings with an iron will, and she pitied him deeply.

One afternoon Jane sat in the schoolroom and, for her own pleasure, painted a careful portrait of Rosamond Oliver, with her golden curls and lovely eyes. St John came in, stood over her shoulder and gazed at the picture for a long time, with a look that held both longing and pain. Then he tore a narrow strip from the clean paper beside it, put it in his pocket without a word and went away.

A few days later, on a night when the snow lay deep on the moor, he came to her cottage, stamped the white from his boots and sat down by the fire. He asked her to tell him her real name, and he held up the strip of paper, on which she had unthinkingly written her signature on the margin. It bore, in her own hand, the words Jane Eyre, which she had written without a thought one idle afternoon.

Jane, startled and silent, admitted at last that it was her true name, and St John then explained that a lawyer in London, a Mr Briggs, had been searching all over England for a girl of that name. Her uncle, John Eyre, who had been a rich wine merchant in Madeira, had died a short time ago and had left every penny of his fortune to his niece. The sum that her uncle had left her was no less than twenty thousand pounds, a fortune beyond anything she had dreamed.

She asked how it was that he, of all people, had heard of it, and for the first time she saw him smile, a quiet and serious smile that changed his face. He told her that John Eyre had been the brother of his own mother, and that the family had long been estranged, so that his sisters and he had never inherited from him. Jane was therefore not only a rich woman but also his cousin, and Diana and Mary were her cousins too.

Jane laughed and wept at once, for she had never in her whole life had a family, and now she had three cousins, a home and an income, all in a single evening. She declared that the fortune must be divided into four equal parts, five thousand pounds for each of the cousins, since she cared more for kindred than for gold. They protested for a while, but in the end, seeing her determination, they gave in.

At Christmas the cousins gathered together at Moor House, and Jane, who had waited all her life for such a thing, scrubbed the floors, baked the pies and decorated the rooms with holly. The old house became bright and warm and full of laughter, and the cousins sat round the fire in the evening, reading, talking and telling stories. Jane felt that she had at last found her true home, and that no one could ever take it from her.

In the spring she closed her school, and the village girls came to say goodbye with gifts of flowers, while the lovely Rosamond wept openly at the loss of her friend. St John, who was preparing to leave for the East, began to teach Jane the language of Hindustani, and he worked with her for hours each evening, stern, patient and exacting. She learned quickly, though she felt all the while that his cool, steady gaze was measuring her at every step.

After some weeks he told her gravely that he wished her to marry him and come with him to India as a missionary's wife, because he believed she was fitted for such work. He did not pretend to love her, he said, but he thought that God had formed her for labour and not for love, and that it was her duty to say yes. Jane felt the earnest force of his will bearing down upon her, and her heart grew heavy and troubled within her.

She replied that she would gladly go to India with him as his sister, but that she could never marry a man who did not love her, and she would not take a husband in the name of duty. He grew cold and stern, but he knelt in prayer with his hand upon her head, and she felt her resistance beginning to melt under the power of his voice. She asked Heaven, almost in tears, to show her what was right, and to give her strength to do it.

As she spoke, the whole room seemed to shake, and she felt a sensation like an electric shock pass through her heart, and then she heard a voice that was not St John's and not of any living person near. Three times it called her name, Jane, Jane, Jane, and she knew in an instant that it was Mr Rochester's, and that it came from far, far away. She cried out that she was coming, and she begged him to wait for her, wherever he might be.

In the morning Jane told St John calmly that she had heard a call that could not be ignored, and that she must find out what had become of Mr Rochester before she could decide anything. St John said that she was acting under a strange excitement, but she assured him that she was perfectly calm, and then she set out on her journey. The coach carried her northward through a night and a day, while she listened to the beating of her own heart.

At last she stepped down at the inn near Thornfield, left her small trunk there and hurried across the fields toward the house that she had once thought of as her home. She had been tormenting herself with fears all the way, but as she came round the last bend and saw the gate, she stopped as though she had been struck. Where the great house had stood, there was now only a black and roofless ruin, with empty windows staring at the sky.

She went back to the inn and, taking a seat in a quiet corner, asked the landlord what had happened, though she could hardly bear to hear it. He told her that the house had burned to the ground the previous autumn, when a madwoman who lived on the third floor had set it alight in the dead of night. She had climbed onto the roof, he said, and had cried out and thrown herself down, and she had died on the ground below.

Mr Rochester, he said, had behaved like a hero, for he had led the servants safely out and then had gone back to find his wife, and a falling beam had struck him. He had lost the sight of both his eyes, and one of his hands had been so badly crushed that it had to be taken off. Now he lived alone, some thirty miles away, in a dark and lonely house in the forest called Ferndean, with only two old servants to help him.

Jane hired a post-chaise at once, and as the daylight faded and the road grew darker, she was driven through miles of damp and silent woods to a lonely house with no light at all. Ferndean was a very old building, half hidden among the trees, with narrow windows, and an air of damp and desertion hung about it. At the door an old woman named Mary stared at the stranger in amazement and did not know what to say.

Mary was just carrying a tray with a candle and a glass of water into the parlour, so Jane took it from her hands and went in, with her heart beating heavily. By a low and dying fire sat a figure that she knew, his head bowed and his hands clasped before him, and Pilot lay at his feet. The man did not move or look up, and she saw the dark and blinded face that had once been so full of life.

She spoke his name, and he started up and cried out, asking whether it was a dream, or a spirit, or whether it was really his Jane who stood before him. She took his hand, and he put out his other arm, which was scarred and bare, and felt her face and shoulders and hair, and then he drew her to him with a cry. He said that he must be dreaming, and that he would wake in the old darkness.

Later he said, in a sad voice, that she must pity him, that he was a blind and broken man, and that she should look for a better husband than a cripple. Jane knelt beside his chair, took his hand and told him that she was free and rich, that her uncle had left her a fortune, and that she was her own mistress. She would be his neighbour, his nurse, his housekeeper, his companion, and she would never leave him again.

He asked her then, with something of the old fire in his voice, whether she would be his wife, and she said yes, with all her heart and all her soul. They were married quietly a few days later in the old church, with only the clerk and a few villagers there to see it, and no one else had been told. At the end of that quiet day Jane gave the news to her reader in the plainest possible words, “Reader, I married him.”

For ten years now, Jane writes, she has lived in the deepest happiness with the man she loves, and neither of them has ever known a quarrel. Their first son was born two years after the wedding, and when Mr Rochester held him, he found that his sight had come back enough to see the child's dark eyes, which were the same as his own. St John, in the meantime, is still in India, labouring bravely in the face of illness, and his last letter says that his work will soon be over, and he is ready for his reward.
